sources.title: Tibo's 12-step playbook for taking SaaS apps to $100K MRR
sources.originalTitle: I Built 4 SaaS Apps to $100K MRR: Here's My Exact Playbook
sources.summary: Tibo walks through the repeatable 12-step process behind four SaaS apps passing $100K MRR. The core idea: ship MVPs in days, talk daily to relevant users until retention is sticky, then go broad on distribution and double down on one or two channels. He also explains why he runs a portfolio of products.

principles.text: Build the MVP in days or weeks using shortcuts like no-code and boilerplates, since most ideas fail.
principles.quote: You will have a 90% failure rate. It's same for me, it's the same for a lot of people that I know.

principles.text: Get feedback only from 5-10 people who are your real target audience; irrelevant feedback, good or bad, is worthless.
principles.quote: If the person is not relevant, like there is absolutely no point in listening to this feedback, either positive or negative.

principles.text: Route support to your personal DMs and fix issues in minutes until a product hits $10K/month; fast responsiveness creates customers for life.
principles.quote: until each product is making 10 K per month in revenue, the supports link on each software is directing people to my Twitter DMs.

principles.text: Be the user of your own product to build features that solve real user problems and understand the core pain.
principles.quote: I'm being the user of my own products. And by doing that, I'm 10 times more relevant with understanding the core problem and giving a proper solution.

principles.text: Don't scale acquisition before retention; iterate until users can't live without it, and treat complaints as a sign of commitment.
principles.quote: If you go abroad, like if you focus on acquisition and at the same time have a low retention, you will spend a lot of energy pushing people to your software, and 99% of those people are going to flow away directly after trying your software.

principles.text: Scale with SEO, ads and affiliates once you have stickiness, then go all in on the one or two channels that work and kill the rest.
principles.quote: in the end, my experience is for each software, growth is pretty much about one or two acquisition channels. Those two acquisition channels, I'm going all in on them.

sources.title: How Tibo Louis-Lucas bootstrapped 5 AI products to $1M+/month: ship fast, charge early, SEO tools
sources.originalTitle: How This Solo AI Founder Bootstrapped 5 Products to 1M+ / Month | Tibo Louis-Lucas
sources.summary: Tibo explains how he runs five AI businesses with a tiny team: validate with revenue from day one, ship many cheap experiments, stay in constant contact with users, and follow unexpected usage into pivots (product videos to Rabbit). He covers pricing at $50-100/month, churn thresholds, tool-based SEO, and building with AI in Cursor.

principles.text: Don't force-sell to avoid being wrong; stay open to signals that a bigger opportunity exists and pivot.
principles.quote: it's more important for them to not be wrong than being successful. And so what you do in these cases you're trying to force sell.

principles.text: Talk to users constantly; when people twist your product into another use, follow that signal.
principles.quote: When you have a product that is made for one thing and people are actually twisting it to turn into this other thing, that's usually a very strong signal that you have to follow.

principles.text: Validate with revenue from day one; without sticky revenue, other signals are self-deception.
principles.quote: if there is no revenue, there's no stickiness in the revenue, it's going to be very hard to build a successful business.

principles.text: Price at $50-100/month to attract high-quality, low-churn customers and position as premium, not cheap.
principles.quote: I feel that's the perfect amount from 50 to 100 per month because it's not too much, so people do not ask me for quotes before signing up

principles.text: Monthly churn above ~20% means the product isn't sticky; fix retention before investing in acquisition.
principles.quote: I would consider everything um better than than 20% churn, like monthly churn.

principles.text: Ship many small experiments quickly; quantity of attempts leads to better outcomes than polishing one.
principles.quote: we were shipping one new project per per week uh until something stick.

sources.title: How Tibo built Tweet Hunter and Taplio to an 8-figure exit: ship weekly, partner with creators, SEO tools
sources.originalTitle: He built an 8-figure AI startup (and got banned from LinkedIn)
sources.summary: Tibo explains how he and his co-founder shipped about 10 products in four months, hit on Tweet Hunter, then used creator equity partnerships and free SEO mini tools to grow Taplio. He also covers building for yourself, an earn-out heavy acquisition, and the LinkedIn ban.

principles.text: Fail fast by shipping a new product every week and moving on if it brings no revenue within a few weeks.
principles.quote: we started shipping a new product every week and it was like if it doesn't work like if if it doesn't bring some Revenue in just a few weeks we just go to the next product

sources.title: How Tibo built 40 SEO mini tools for Tapo and Tweet Hunter, and why he bets on anti-AI positioning
sources.originalTitle: Creator tools you can build that will print money
sources.summary: Tibo Louis-Lucas explains how a steady stream of free SEO mini tools drove most of Tapo and Tweet Hunter's traffic. He covers the Vidio-style pattern of tools that drop users straight into the main product, why tool searches should survive AI search, and why "no AI" positioning is an uncrowded arbitrage. He also pitches a brand-sponsorship page business built on moderation.

principles.text: Ship a steady stream of free SEO mini tools; together they became the majority of traffic.
principles.quote: we built more than one per month so at the end we had like 40 SE optimized mini tools

principles.text: Winners are unpredictable and low-intent keywords can still pay off: a quick LinkedIn video downloader out-ranked the researched tools.
principles.quote: it was a very low intent uh keyword for Tapo but super high traffic a million per month uh visitors super crazy

principles.text: Make each mini tool a feature of the main product so users land inside it with no signup.
principles.quote: they redirects to their main tool like vid doio and you are actually inside the tool without even signing up without paying for anything

principles.text: Action-based searches (find a tool to do X) will keep going to Google, so the mini-tool strategy holds up against AI search.
principles.quote: if you are looking for a tool uh to compress a video or to download a video from LinkedIn it's very unlikely to me that you're going to query that on tgbt because you are looking for a tool

principles.text: Anti-AI, human-made positioning is an under-crowded opening while AI niches are saturated.
principles.quote: the product itself is an anti- AI uh positioning because using this tool you are like certified to be a genuine human using a tool by hand

principles.text: In a seemingly saturated marketplace, the unsolved pain (sorting inbound applicants) is the product to build.
principles.quote: we got hundreds of application that it became a nightmare to sort them and to to spot the good ones so that's that's the real issue to solve

sources.title: How Tibo built Tweet Hunter, sold for $8M, then ran five co-maker startups past $400k/month
sources.originalTitle: I sold my startup for $8M. Then built 5 more making $400k+/month.
sources.summary: Tibo explains his shift from ego-driven, VC-funded failures to building revenue-first products. He covers the equity-for-influencer launch that took Tweet Hunter from 3K to 20K MRR in two weeks and his co-maker model of rescuing stuck products with distribution. He also shares retention lessons from Outrank and what he'd change in an exit.

principles.text: Build for revenue and a good living, not to impress people; chasing ego metrics hid the fact that nothing was working.
principles.quote: just trying to make a good living out of the product we're building.

principles.text: Give a big influencer real equity as a co-founder and let them launch it to their audience; it can multiply MRR in weeks.
principles.quote: just this launch, I think in two weeks, we got from 3K in monthly revenue to 20K.

principles.text: Market the outcome (more business, more money), not the feature layer; it multiplied conversion.
principles.quote: And by by embracing that approach and just changing a little bit our marketing, it worked like 10 times more.

principles.text: Partner on others' stuck products: motivation is higher on their own idea. Fix the core with a few users, then add distribution.
principles.quote: if you reach out on an existing project, it's his ID. Like the the guy is going to be crazy motivated no matter what because it's it's his ID.

principles.text: Talk to users directly to learn their workflow, then design the product so it works without discipline from them (auto-publish).
principles.quote: If you do not come to the software, no matter what, it's going to be published anyway.

principles.text: Validate by building a prototype in days and putting it in front of relevant users rather than describing the idea.
principles.quote: it's 10 times more efficient when you have an idea to quickly build it in two days and put it in the hands of people who are relevant to use this ID and give you feedback.

sources.title: How Tibo shipped 11 products in 4 months, found Tweet Hunter, and grew it 7x to a multi-million exit
sources.originalTitle: Build fast, launch fast, fail fast: The real founder playbook | Thibault (Tibo) Louis-Lucas
sources.summary: Tibo recounts two failed startups, then a "fail in two weeks, not two years" approach: ship a product a week and judge only by revenue. That led to Tweet Hunter (the 11th product), built on his own problem and grown through building in public, SEO and an influencer partner, then sold on a 20% upfront / 80% milestone deal. He also covers owning your audience via newsletters, AI shifting value to distribution, and partnering with makers instead of hiring.

principles.text: Fail fast: ship a new product every week and judge it by revenue alone, not vanity metrics.
principles.quote: if we need to fail again it it needs to be in two weeks and not in two years and so we started this process of trying to ship a new product every week or so until something actually sticken until we get Revenue

principles.text: Build for your own problems; you only deeply understand the core need of problems you live yourself.
principles.quote: I would really start building something for yourself first because you are an expert on your own problems like building a good product is in the first place a true understanding of the problem that you are solving

principles.text: Free users without paying conversion are not a real business; revenue is the signal.
principles.quote: if people do not convert to paid user you don't have a real product like you don't have a real business

principles.text: Building in public earns trust, which brings feedback, sales and promotion. Sharing tips gets you the credit.
principles.quote: if you are the guy sharing the tips you get something what that that is amazing today which is trust and by by doing that by sharing value every day on Twitter by just sharing tips by showing true numbers what happens is people start trusting you

principles.text: Don't rely on social platforms alone: you don't own followers. Own a newsletter list, and keep exportable backups.
principles.quote: you do not own your followers you do not own your um like your accounts it can just get suspended at any time what you truly own is a newsletter subscriber base

principles.text: As AI drives build costs toward zero, value shifts to distribution, storytelling and educating users.
principles.quote: building cost are slowly going to zero ... the value will be in distribution in your capability to distribute an existing product and to create a nice story telling about it and to educate people on how to use product properly

sources.title: How Tibo shipped 10 failed products, then built Tweet Hunter and a $1M/month SaaS portfolio
sources.originalTitle: From 10 Failed Products to a $1M/Month SaaS Portfolio
sources.summary: Tibo Louis-Lucas explains his revenue-first validation approach, shipping a product a week until one stuck, going deep on a single platform, and giving product-level equity to influencers for distribution. He also covers why he now avoids selling, uses DMs over calls, and runs five product-led SaaS solo with AI.

principles.text: Validation means paying customers, not free users or usage.
principles.quote: the number one mistake that most people do is thinking that having some usage of your product, having some free users is validation

principles.text: Ship a new product every week until one sticks, and never spend years on an unvalidated idea.
principles.quote: ship one new product every week until something stick.

principles.text: Beat saturated horizontal tools by going full depth on one platform for individuals.
principles.quote: we just integrated one social media, Twitter, but we went like full depth on on this one.

principles.text: Give a distribution partner a product-level share (profit and exit) so they are strongly incentivized to promote.
principles.quote: we gave away 25% of the product to a Twitter influencer who would be like the the head of distribution

principles.text: Treat promoters like investors, with no obligation to promote and regular financial updates; most still promote.
principles.quote: they were really not used to being treated as investors.

principles.text: Learn from DM conversations with early users rather than public launch announcements; avoid calls to protect focus.
principles.quote: it's more about like having a real conversation with people when they're trying your product.

sources.title: How Tibo built and sold Tweet Hunter in 18 months: ship fast, solve your own problem, skip VC
sources.originalTitle: How to Go From $0 to a 7 Figure Exit in 18 Months | Tibo Louis-Lucas
sources.summary: Tibo explains how, after two VC-funded failures, he and his co-founder shipped about one product a week until Tweet Hunter took off, then sold it with a revenue-linked earn-out. He covers building for your own pain, DM-driven support as marketing, influencer co-founders, free tools for SEO, and surviving platform risk.

principles.text: Validate by shipping a new product every week and drop what doesn't earn revenue, instead of spending two years on one unproven idea.
principles.quote: we went from um spending two years on an ID that could be like invalidated leading to a huge loss of time to this idea of running of building one new products per week and to just try to validate it as fast as possible

principles.text: Build for your own problem. Being the first customer helps you tell real value from nice-to-have features and makes many others likely share the pain.
principles.quote: if you are the first customer and if you are building something for you it's it's very likely that tons of other people are having the same problem

principles.text: Stay in one space and solve the same people's real problems for a long time. Chasing trends and building from assumptions produces ideas that sound good but aren't businesses.
principles.quote: try to build relentlessly for the same people trying to solve the same problem

principles.text: Fast, founder-led support is marketing. Fixing a bug within minutes of a DM made users tweet about the speed and gave an early boost.
principles.quote: the thing that was that would blow the user's mind was actually to have the DM trying to fix it in like five minutes pushing it

principles.text: Build in public and ship many free single-purpose tools. They rank on Google for specific queries and bring steady traffic.
principles.quote: we built tons and tons of free minitos that have the purpose of of serving one specific need

principles.text: Product-market fit is unmistakable and painful; if you have to wonder whether it's working, it probably isn't yet.
principles.quote: when you know you know like when it happens you know when it doesn't happen you never know

sources.title: How Tibo shipped a product a week to find Tweet Hunter and what he learned
sources.originalTitle: Ep 66 | Ship One New Product Every Week Until Something Sticks (w/ Tibo Louis-Lucas)
sources.summary: Tibo recounts how two failed early startups taught him to validate with payments, build hands-on, and ship fast. He then describes shipping one product a week until Tweet Hunter took off, and how a viral partner launch drove growth to an acquisition.

principles.text: Ship a new product every week and collect feedback until one sticks.
principles.quote: we would try to ship um one new product every week until something stick. uh it was early 2021 and I think in four months we shipped something like 10 or 11 projects.

principles.text: Validate demand through payments, not free usage. Going free only proves people will use it for nothing.
principles.quote: The validation comes from the payments. Meaning like if people pay, I get my product validated, but I want to prove that people are willing to pay for it and not even use it for free.

principles.text: Don't delegate the hard startup work; staying hands-on with product and marketing is what matters.
principles.quote: I was basically u delegating the most difficult task of a startup which is creating the product, understanding what people want and and even marketing the product.

principles.text: Fix your own problem: you are the expert on it, and many others likely share it.
principles.quote: try to fix your own issue. You you are basically an expert on your own problems, you understand them better than anyone else.

principles.text: Build what people actually want, not how you wish the world worked.
principles.quote: the product that works, they do what people want. They do not do what the founder would like the world to work that way.

principles.text: Growth comes from relentless daily shipping and talking to users, not a single big move.
principles.quote: almost every day we were adding a few features, almost every week we were shipping um a free tool to try to rank on some SEO keywords.

sources.title: How Tibo built and sold SaaS for $8M: ship weekly, charge early, build distribution
sources.originalTitle: How to make $10M from a SaaS
sources.summary: Tibo Louis-Lucas explains how he shipped a product a week to find product-market fit, validated only by revenue, and sold Tweet Hunter and Taplio for about $8M. He covers a 25% profit-share deal with an influencer, free mini-tools for SEO, buying SaaS for distribution, and starting to build with AI.

principles.text: Validate only with revenue; free users and kind feedback are not product-market fit.
principles.quote: validation is about people paying for the product it's not about free users or people telling you that you have a great idea

principles.text: Ship a product per week for one target and one problem, ideally one you have yourself, to shorten time to product-market fit.
principles.quote: we wanted to shorten the time to product Market fits and so that's how we got into this idea of shipping one product per per week until something stick

principles.text: Ship more: quantity beats quality since you can't predict winners; carve out time weekly for new shots.
principles.quote: increase your shots on goal by carving out at least 20% of your time to just work on new things take new shots

principles.text: Give an influencer a profit share on one product, tied to marketing ownership, to bootstrap distribution; be fully transparent on numbers.
principles.quote: GK would have the marketing ownership and responsibilities of promoting tweet Center he would have to uh actively work on the product and to actively promote it with campaigns referal program and and some other stuff and in exchange he would have 25% of the monthly profit

principles.text: Unbundle product features into free one-page mini tools; they rank on Google and compound as an acquisition channel.
principles.quote: we basically took features of the products and we extracted them and put them in a simple onepage onepage tool

principles.text: As AI makes software cheap to build, value shifts to distribution, so buy SaaS and invest in audience.
principles.quote: it's going to come from your distribution and so that's why I'm I'm also buying s and focusing on distribution myself

sources.title: How Tibo Louis-Lucas bootstrapped Tweet Hunter to a $10M exit and now builds with equity partners
sources.originalTitle: I Sold My Bootstrapped Startup for $10 MILLION
sources.summary: Tibo explains why he left venture-backed teams for lean bootstrapping: ship a product a week, follow revenue only, and kill what doesn't work. He covers equity-sharing with creators, an earn-out sale structure, the new modes in the AI era, and his equity-partnership model of buying or partnering on small products.

principles.text: Judge ideas by revenue, not free users or compliments; kill products that miss your revenue threshold.
principles.quote: revenue was the only uh metric that we were following to decide if we would continue or shift to another ID

sources.title: How Tibo built $1M/month SaaS products with zero original ideas
sources.originalTitle: How He Built $1M/Month SaaS Business with Zero Original Ideas - Tibo Maker (Thibault LOUIS-LUCAS)
sources.outlet: Authority in the Wild with Gabe Marusca
sources.summary: Tibo explains how he validates ideas by shipping many products fast, building tools he uses himself, and making each one 10x better at a single thing. He also covers single-price pricing, affiliates, user DMs for feedback, and why distribution compounds across a product portfolio.

principles.text: Validate by shipping a new product every week until something sticks, instead of polishing one idea for years.
principles.quote: the thing that I did when I when I got back to startuping is try to ship one new product every week until something actually stick.

principles.text: Ideas aren't the edge. Make the product 10x better at one specific thing than competitors.
principles.quote: my edge is building great products um that are like at least 10 times better at a specific thing compared to the competition

principles.text: Be great at one thing that users value; being average at everything else is fine.
principles.quote: You have to do one thing extremely well like you have to be great at one thing and then you can be just average or good at everything else.

principles.text: Build products you use yourself daily so you fix real friction and understand the core need.
principles.quote: build products where I am the users. By doing that, I was able to use the product every single day and to solve all the little friction that I had

principles.text: Audience follows success, not the reverse. Validation needs only a few DMs and replies, not thousands of followers.
principles.quote: I have a big audience because I had a successful product.

principles.text: Offer one price or an obvious no-brainer choice; higher prices attract more serious, loyal customers.
principles.quote: the more choices you offer to users, the harder it is for them to actually um convert and subscribe.

sources.title: How Tibo Louis-Lucas built and sold Tweet Hunter and Taplio: ship fast, charge early, stay lean
sources.originalTitle: Lancer vite, échouer, recommencer : l’histoire de Tweet Hunter et Taplio - Tibo Louis-Lucas
sources.summary: Tibo explains why two VC-backed startups failed (no focus on revenue, big teams that couldn't pivot) and how he then shipped about 10 small projects in 4 months to find Tweet Hunter. He covers charging early, giving creators a small product stake for distribution, SEO mini-tools, and structuring the exit.

principles.text: Judge a business by revenue, not vanity metrics like signups; users who don't pay are false reassurance.
principles.quote: you are not revenue-driven, you are not 100% focused on revenue (translated from French)

principles.text: Raising money and hiring a big team blocks fast pivots; staying solo or tiny lets you test ideas quickly.
principles.quote: raising money and hiring a big team completely stops you from pivoting quickly and working on the latest idea you had (translated from French)

principles.text: Compress a two-year failure into a week by shipping many tiny products fast and killing what doesn't earn.
principles.quote: the goal was to try to compress those 2 years into one week (translated from French)

principles.text: Ask for payment very early on every product, since willingness to pay is the real validation.
principles.quote: very, very early in the process, on every product, we asked people to pay (translated from French)

principles.text: Create distribution when small by giving big creators a tiny stake in the product with no formal obligations.
principles.quote: we told them: we give you 0.1% of Tweet Hunter, and in exchange you have no concrete obligation (translated from French)

principles.text: Build free SEO mini-tools from your product's features; their traffic compounds over time and feeds the main product.
principles.quote: the traffic from these mini tools will compound and become more and more important (translated from French)

sources.title: Why Tibo is doubling down on SuperX: building the X growth tool he needed himself
sources.originalTitle: Ready for growth on X?
sources.summary: Tibo explains why he bought out SuperX's co-founder, spent six months in stealth rebuilding it, and bet on X over LinkedIn after selling Tweet Hunter and Taplio. He argues growth on X needs good content plus a small circle of supportive friends, and that building for your own need produces a useful product.

principles.text: Growth on X rests on two things: good content and a support network of friends.
principles.quote:
The current SuperX product comes from realizing what you need to grow on X:

- Good content

- Friends (your support network)

principles.text: Seed growth with about 10 highly supportive people who engage with everything you post.
principles.quote: You need a foundation of 10 incredibly supportive people who will like and engage with everything you do.

principles.text: Build something you desperately need yourself; daily personal use validates the product.
principles.quote:
The product works. The foundations are solid. I'm using it daily and seeing results.

This is what happens when you build something you desperately need yourself.

principles.text: Slow shipping of basic features is a competitive weakness; rivals who ship in days win users.
principles.quote: When X launched long-form posts, Tweet Hunter took multiple months to implement it. Competitors had it in days.

principles.text: A browser extension alone limits growth; a full web app is needed to scale.
principles.quote: We built the extension and it was quite successful. But I felt like it was hard to grow with just a Twitter extension. We needed a web app.

principles.text: When foundations are weak, accept a full revamp and work in stealth rather than rushing out a weak product.
principles.quote:
But we realized some foundations weren't there. We needed a complete revamp.

So we worked in stealth mode for 6 months.

sources.title: Tibo's 7-step playbook for building a business in 2025
sources.originalTitle: 7 steps to building a business
sources.summary: Tibo lays out a seven-step path from finding your edge to fixing retention. Ideas, not building, are the bottleneck now, so validate demand with a fake landing page, build in one week, find the real problem, scale acquisition fast, then obsess over retention.

principles.text: Business success starts with being better than others at something; find your unfair advantage first.
principles.quote: “You have to be better than others at something.”

principles.text: Building is no longer the bottleneck; knowing what to build is. Collect ideas from complaints and requests.
principles.quote: Building is not a bottleneck any more. Knowing what to build is.

principles.text: Validate demand before coding: a landing page with an email input. No emails, skip the idea.
principles.quote: If people drop their email = validation. No interest? Skip to next idea.

principles.text: Force a one-week build constraint to narrow to the core value proposition, then ship to real people.
principles.quote: Why!? 👉 It will force your to narrow it down to its core value proposition.

principles.text: The problem you think you solve is usually not the real one; most reduce to money, health, or relationships/status.
principles.quote: The problem you think you're solving usually isn't the real one.

principles.text: Retention matters more than acquisition; it is how a business compounds.
principles.quote: Retention > acquisition.

sources.title: How to find a $1M SaaS idea: the math, the 10% rule, and 2-week validation
sources.originalTitle: How to find a $1M SaaS idea
sources.summary: Tibo breaks a $1M SaaS down to roughly 350-700 paying customers, argues that copying the same idea-finding process as everyone else gives you the same ideas, and recommends building many products with strict 2-week validation windows. He gives four go/no-go questions and a fit test for choosing an idea.

principles.text: A $1M valuation is just 350 customers at $100/month or 700 at $50/month; the idea only needs to find that many consistent payers.
principles.quote: Your idea doesn't need to change the world. It just needs to find 350 to 700 people who will pay you consistently every month.

principles.text: If your idea-finding process matches everyone else's, you'll get the same ideas and compete with everyone who saw the same trend.
principles.quote: If you have the same process as everyone else, you'll have the same ideas as everyone else.

principles.text: Founders with deep industry experience see broken things others accept as normal; without that, use a build-many process instead.
principles.quote: Your industry knowledge makes you see something obviously broken that everyone else has accepted as normal.

principles.text: Expect about a 10% success rate on new products, so never go all in on one idea; build many instead.
principles.quote: Your success rate when creating new products will probably be 10% at best.

principles.text: Shipping one product per week forces you to ship over plan, get fast feedback, and discard the garbage cheaply.
principles.quote: It works because it forces you to ship instead of plan, get real feedback fast, and move past the 80% that will be garbage before it costs you a year of your life.

principles.text: Pick ideas that fit your skills, enjoyment, longevity, and the marketing channel you're naturally good at (SEO, content, ads, or sales).
principles.quote: if you hate writing and hate SEO, building a product that lives or dies on those channels will drain you fast.

sources.title: Why SaaS pricing should start from the price point: avoid the low-price trap and price for results
sources.originalTitle: What is the ideal pricing for a SaaS
sources.summary: Tibo argues SaaS founders should work backwards from a price range ($29-$99) rather than use psychological pricing tricks. Low prices signal low quality, and raising Tweet Hunter from $9 to $49 cut conversion slightly but lowered churn and raised LTV. Price for the results delivered to people who badly need them.

principles.text: Work backwards from the price point: pick a price range first, then decide what to build and how.
principles.quote: You work backwards from the price point.

principles.text: Low prices don't attract more customers long-term; they signal low quality, and the planned later price rise never comes.
principles.quote: Here's the truth: Later never comes.

principles.text: High-value customers don't care about price if the product solves a burning problem; a low price can't make up for low value.
principles.quote: A low price DOESN'T compensate for delivering LOW value.

principles.text: Raising prices cuts conversion a little but lowers churn; the LTV bump offset the conversion drop every time at Tweet Hunter.
principles.quote: EVERY SINGLE TIME we raised prices, the LTV bump made for the conversion drop.

principles.text: Complainers about price are often your most reliant users; the real churn is silent cancellations from people who see no value.
principles.quote: People who complain often LOVE your product

principles.text: Price for results, target people who value them, don't fear raising prices, and build premium to charge premium.
principles.quote: Price for results, not features

sources.title: How Tibo grew five SaaS products from $125k to $700k+ MRR in 2025
sources.originalTitle: 5.6x Revenue Growth in 1 year (My 2025 Review)
sources.summary: Tibo's 2025 review of his multi-product portfolio, which grew 5.6x to $700k+ MRR. Product by product, he draws lessons on building tailwind businesses, turning customers into a growth loop, cutting losers, finding co-founders, and building a real audience over vanity followers.

principles.text: Build a 'tailwind business' that gets better every time the underlying AI/tech improves, instead of fearing new models.
principles.quote: Revid is a “Tailwind business” meaning it will get better, sharper when a new + better AI model works in the background.

principles.text: Don't just wrap APIs: build workflows users need, focus on quality niches, and add platform integrations that create switching costs.
principles.quote: We're not just wrapping AI APIs - we built workflows users actually need (without playing with AI on their own)

principles.text: Make customers an active part of your growth loop; network effects (like a backlink exchange pool) improve retention.
principles.quote: “How can I make my customers an active part of my growth journey? Can this help them too?”

principles.text: Distribute revenue across several products so no single product carries the business; it changes how you take risks.
principles.quote: Revenue became genuinely distributed for the first time. I'm no longer dependent on a single product carrying everything.

principles.text: If a product stagnates and you can't crack growth, hand it to someone who can focus on it instead of holding on.
principles.quote: Sometimes the best move is giving a great product to someone who can focus on it properly.

principles.text: The right co-founder fills the skill gaps you lack; a rebuild and relaunch with better storytelling unstuck a $1k MRR product.
principles.quote: The right co-founder changes everything. Rob brought the missing piece I couldn't provide alone.

sources.title: How Tibo copies crowded markets to build a $1M MRR portfolio
sources.originalTitle: How to copy your way to $1M
sources.summary: Tibo argues bootstrapped founders should skip "blue ocean" invention and instead rebuild an existing product for the user the market leader ignores. He gives a three-question framework for picking where to compete and cites Mark Pincus's repeat-copy playbook.

principles.text: Don't hunt for untouched markets. Pick a crowded market and serve the user type being ignored.
principles.quote: I didn't find new, untouched markets. I found crowded markets with one type of user being ignored and built something better for them.

principles.text: Blue-ocean invention suits VCs who can absorb 99 losses, not bootstrappers with limited attempts.
principles.quote: For you as a founder, if your number of attempts is limited, one loss can be dramatic.

principles.text: Ask what the best version looks like for the person the market leader ignores.
principles.quote: What does the best possible version of this look like for the person being ignored by the current market leader?

principles.text: Only pursue problems people already pay to solve; no payers means insufficient pain.
principles.quote: Who is already paying for a solution to this problem? If nobody is paying, the problem is not painful enough. Full stop.

principles.text: Find the gap every leader leaves: segments they ignore because they are too big or focused elsewhere.
principles.quote: Every market leader ignores someone. They get too big, too bloated, too focused on a certain kind of client. That gap is where you live.

principles.text: Define the one thing that would make that user switch immediately, and be meaningfully better at it.
principles.quote: What would make that person switch today? Not eventually. Immediately. That's your one thing to be meaningfully better at.

sources.title: Why Tibo won't raise VC again: user validation beats investor validation
sources.originalTitle: I’ll never raise VC money again.
sources.summary: Tibo explains why he, having raised VC before, now bootstraps: investor money creates fake validation, VC power-law math pushes you toward lottery-ticket growth instead of a free profitable business, and most internet companies only need paying users. He reports $1M MRR across 5 bootstrapped, profitable products.

principles.text: Investor money is not market validation; only paying customers validate a product.
principles.quote: VC money is not user validation. It never was. The only validation that matters is someone opening their wallet and paying for your product.

principles.text: Raising is the start of the work, not an achievement worth celebrating.
principles.quote: Congratulating a founder on raising is like congratulating a chef on getting the vegetables.

principles.text: VCs optimise for a 100x lottery ticket, not your sustainable profitable business, so decent growth can lose their support.
principles.quote: They expect 9/10 of their bets to fail. They need just one company per fund to return everything.

principles.text: VC pressure shifts you from building for users to chasing the next round, costing freedom.
principles.quote: You stop building for users and start working just to raise the next round.

principles.text: Bootstrapped, cash-generating products remove exit pressure and give freedom to move fast or slow.
principles.quote: When you bootstrap, and your products print cash, there's no pressure to exit.

principles.text: Raise only when scale precedes revenue (infrastructure) or compliance costs are huge; otherwise get paying users.
principles.quote: But most internet businesses don't need it. You need users who pay. That's the only math that matters.

sources.title: How Outrank went from $300 to $300k MRR: repositioning, backlink network effects, and owning the narrative
sources.originalTitle: How we turned $300 into $3 million
sources.summary: Tibo explains how he and co-founder Eugene took Outrank from a $300 MRR AI blog generator to $300k MRR in 15 months. The keys were repositioning as SEO infrastructure, building a backlink exchange network as a moat, and flipping the "AI killed SEO" fear into a growth narrative.

principles.text: Positioning beats features: reframing the same product can change the whole outcome.
principles.quote: The lesson: Positioning beats features every time.

principles.text: A commodity (AI content) has no moat; network effects such as a contextual backlink exchange turn it into one.
principles.quote: The lesson: Network effects turn commodities into moats.

principles.text: Position into the market's fear rather than away from it; the winning narrative gets the customers.
principles.quote: The lesson: Position into the fear, not away from it.

principles.text: Different growth levers work at different stages: distribution early, product results and testimonials in the middle, narrative late.
principles.quote: What works at $10k MRR doesn't work at $200k MRR.

principles.text: Keep pricing stupid simple: one plan, no credits, no tiers, no confusion.
principles.quote: $99/month for 30 articles. No credits. No tiers. No confusion.

principles.text: The builder's playbook: find the moat, own the narrative, move fast.
principles.quote: Find the moat. Own the narrative. Move fast.

sources.title: How Tibo keeps customers forever: filter requests, raise prices, build moats
sources.originalTitle: How I keep my customers forever
sources.summary: Tibo argues retention is a high-margin system that compounds, unlike acquisition, which resets every month. He gives five levers: filter feature requests instead of complying, build systems, raise prices to change who your customer is, make customization a moat, and tie customers' own success to your product.

principles.text: Retention is built once and compounds; acquisition is an expensive sprint you repeat forever.
principles.quote: Retention is different. It's a system you build once. High margin, compounds instead of resetting every month, and it's what actually stacks MRR and builds enterprise value over time.

principles.text: Filter feature requests rather than complying; protect your differentiated workflow and higher-tier value.
principles.quote: Your job as a founder isn't to comply. It's to filter.

principles.text: Saying no to requests that erase your product's difference is why people choose you (Revid skips micro-control for full video generation).
principles.quote: We get a lot of requests asking for more manual control. If we said yes to all of them, we'd become exactly like every other AI video tool out there.

principles.text: Fix categories of problems with systems, not one-off patches, so revenue compounds.
principles.quote: When you solve a user's problem, ask if you just patched one instance or built something that prevents the whole category of problems.

principles.text: Raising prices lowers churn because higher-paying customers have skin in the game and make the product work.
principles.quote: At Tweet Hunter, we started at $9/month. Then we raised it, eventually landing at $49/month. The expected outcome was more churn. The actual outcome was the opposite.

principles.text: Customization and tying users' own results to your product make leaving costly.
principles.quote: The more a user configures a product around their exact workflow, the harder it becomes for them to leave.

sources.title: Tibo's pricing playbook: require a credit card, charge more, A/B test constantly
sources.originalTitle: This pricing advice will make you millions
sources.summary: Tibo explains why his small-team SaaS products require a credit card before a free trial, why a free tier must earn its keep as acquisition cost, and why bootstrapped B2B founders should charge $40-$100/month instead of $9. He also argues for constant one-metric-at-a-time A/B testing and for choosing a model that fits your own constraints.

principles.text: Require a credit card for trials: it filters for serious users and lifts trial-to-paid conversion, at the cost of volume.
principles.quote: Requiring a credit card creates commitment. If you're willing to enter your card, you're not just curious. You're serious about testing it.

principles.text: Prefer 100 serious trials over 1,000 sign-ups who ghost, especially when your team is tiny and can't absorb support load.
principles.quote: I'd rather have 100 serious trials than 1,000 people who sign up and ghost.

principles.text: Judge a free tier by the job it does: acquisition cost if it finds future buyers, charity if it only serves people who never pay.
principles.quote: The question isn't "should we have a free tier?" It's "what job is the free tier doing?"

principles.text: AI products carry real marginal costs, so free tiers must be deliberately limited and tracked against actual conversion data.
principles.quote: Does your free tier bring you people who eventually pay, or just people looking for free stuff?

principles.text: Small teams and indie hackers should charge more, not less. Fewer customers at $99 beat many at $9 and free time to improve the product.
principles.quote: More indie hackers and small teams should make their apps fully paid and charge MORE, not less.

principles.text: A higher price forces higher quality and gives a clean ROI signal. For B2B software, $40-$100/month works well.
principles.quote: $9/month lets you get lazy. $99/month doesn't let you hide.

sources.title: What 7 killed products taught Tibo: recurring use, timing, self-serve, unit economics
sources.originalTitle: I’ve killed more products than most people launch
sources.summary: Tibo walks through seven products he shut down (ProductLift, Tweet Butler, ConvertRec, GeoLeads, AnimStats, Daily Nuggets and others) and the lesson each taught. The recurring themes are daily/weekly use, timing, avoiding custom work, choosing the right customer type, and unit economics. He argues fast, cheap failures are the best education.

principles.text: Build for recurring use. A problem people only have once is not a SaaS.
principles.quote: You can't build a recurring business on something people need once.

principles.text: Monthly subscriptions need daily or weekly use cases; quarterly use causes brutal churn.
principles.quote: Monthly subscriptions need high frequency use cases.

principles.text: Timing can kill a good idea: wait until the underlying technology is ready.
principles.quote: Some ideas are just 2 years too early. That doesn't make them bad ideas. It makes them bad ideas for right now.

principles.text: If every customer needs custom work, you've built an agency, not a product.
principles.quote: If a product can't work without me, it's not a product, it’s a service.

principles.text: Customer type matters more than revenue; keep products self-service and avoid high-touch enterprise clients.
principles.quote: $1k MRR from the wrong customers is worse than $0 MRR.

principles.text: Kill failing products fast; cheap, quick failures are the best education.
principles.quote: Fast failures are cheap education.

sources.title: How social algorithms really work in 2024: circles, engagement and being social
sources.originalTitle: Social media growth in 2024
sources.summary: Tibo explains his model of how Twitter and LinkedIn distribute content: followers matter little, and posts spread circle by circle based on engagement. He draws action points: make engaging content, use short video, and engage with people around you.

principles.text: Platforms are becoming TikTok: follower count matters little, so small accounts can go viral and big ones stay dead.
principles.quote: every platform is becoming TikTok. And your followers don’t matter.

principles.text: Content is distributed circle by circle; it keeps spreading only while each circle's engagement stays above a threshold.
principles.quote: When you post, your content is shown to circle A. If that group interacts with the content, then it’s shown to circle B. If they interact too — it’s shown to circle C and so on.

principles.text: Engagement beats reputation now; make content that hooks people or it never reaches your own audience.
principles.quote: Now, if your content is not engaging enough - it will never reach your audience in the first place.

principles.text: Funnel broad, surface-level social content audiences into a newsletter for deeper conversation.
principles.quote: You can then funnel those people into your newsletter for a deeper conversation.

principles.text: Start short-form video now and repurpose one video across all platforms.
principles.quote:
1 short form vid =

1 Instagram reel + 1 YouTube short + 1 LinkedIn video + 1 Twitter video + 1 TikTok

principles.text: Grow by being social: engaging with people around you builds your Circle A, which unlocks wider reach.
principles.quote: You can’t win in isolation anymore. Engage with people around you and you will feel a boost in your metrics too.

sources.title: Tibo's 15 startup truths: talk to users, ship fast, charge more, execute
sources.originalTitle: 15 Startup Truths You Need To Hear
sources.summary: Tibo, who built Tweet Hunter and Taplio (sold $8m), lists 15 blunt lessons about building a business. The throughline is action over information: talk to users, cut features, ship many products, launch embarrassing V1s, charge more, and ignore ego, courses and fear of competition.

principles.text: Talk to far more users before coding; assumptions are what kill products.
principles.quote: Every successful product I've built started with dozens of conversations. Every failure started with assumptions.

principles.text: Subtract features: fewer, better ones beat a bloated product.
principles.quote: I've never seen a product fail because it did too few things well. I've seen hundreds fail because they did too many things poorly.

principles.text: Ship volume: launch many products because luck comes from repetitions, not coding more.
principles.quote: I launched 10+ products before finding winners. Most people launch 1-2 then quit.

principles.text: Use affiliate programs to amplify existing traction, not to rescue a failing product.
principles.quote: Outrank's affiliate program works because the product already had traction. We amplified existing momentum, we didn't manufacture it from nothing.

principles.text: Competition validates demand; execution speed, marketing and iteration are the real differentiators.
principles.quote: "Someone's already doing this" is a validation signal, not a stop sign.

principles.text: Raise prices: higher prices attract better customers and can lift revenue while lowering churn.
principles.quote: I raised Tweet Hunter prices 5x and revenue doubled while churn decreased. Higher prices attract better customers.

sources.title: How Tibo approaches SaaS acquisition: building trust, due diligence, and making an offer
sources.originalTitle: How to do due diligence and make an offer?
sources.summary: Tibo's playbook for buying SaaS products: open with a genuine compliment, ask easy questions, state buying intent, and follow up patiently. He then covers technical, financial, legal and marketing due diligence, plus tips like creative deal structuring and verifying Stripe data.

principles.text: Start acquisition talks with a genuine compliment to build trust, not threat.
principles.quote: You are not trying to bring the product down or behaving like a shark to acquire the business. You are genuinely impressed by the product and you are taking time to convey how you like it.

principles.text: Begin with easy, low-effort questions; founders love talking about what they built.
principles.quote: Start by asking questions that are easy to answer and require low effort to respond. So don’t ask for full stats/analysis right away.

principles.text: Treat an initial 'No' as normal; stay friendly and follow up without being pushy.
principles.quote: Even if the answer is No, I maintain a friendly relationship and keep the door open for future interactions.

principles.text: Timing matters: founders are more willing to sell when things start going south.
principles.quote: When the product is newly launched or is doing very well, the founders are enjoying and may refuse to sell. But when things start to go south, founders tend to get more willing to talk about selling.

principles.text: Verify financials directly: require Stripe view-only access and spot-check customer billing.
principles.quote: Get access to their Stripe account (this is a deal break for me if they don’t share view-only access).

principles.text: Prefer targets with unexplored acquisition channels, since they leave more growth for you.
principles.quote: The less acquisition channels the seller has explored, the better, as it’s more growth opportunities for you

sources.title: Tibo's rule for scaling SaaS: decide foundations once, optimize execution daily
sources.originalTitle: Why you can’t scale your software business
sources.summary: Tibo explains how he runs 5 products at $1M MRR: lock foundational decisions (price band, customer type, stack, positioning) once, and spend daily effort on execution. He also covers building systems instead of doing tasks, dogfooding, and the four things he optimizes every day.

principles.text: Pick one price band and stop revisiting it; the price decides your customer, funnel, support and churn.
principles.quote: Every product I build sits in the same price range: $40 to $100 per month. I made this decision years ago. I haven't revisited it since.

principles.text: Different price points attract different customers: $10 consumers churn, $50 prosumers need ROI, $500 businesses need hand-holding.
principles.quote: $50/month attracts prosumers who need ROI. They'll stay if you deliver value. They'll leave if you don't.

principles.text: Don't revisit pricing before $100k MRR unless something big happens; adjust only if nobody buys or everyone churns.
principles.quote: Don't revisit pricing until you hit $100k MRR or unless something big happens.

principles.text: Ask whether a task will recur; if so, build a system (agent, hire, automation) instead of doing it by hand.
principles.quote: Stop asking "how do I do this task?" Start asking "how do I make this task run without me?"

principles.text: Build systems before you feel you need them, because by then you're drowning.
principles.quote: Turn these into systems before you think you need to. Because by the time you "need" to, you're already drowning.

principles.text: Dogfood your product constantly; it surfaces problems and becomes the roadmap. If you wouldn't pay for it, fix it.
principles.quote: Dogfooding isn't optional. It's the difference between building features and building solutions.

sources.title: How Tibo sold Tweet Hunter and Taplio for $10M+, then tripled ARR and bought Typeframe
sources.originalTitle: Thibault Louis-Lucas: Selling a $10M SaaS and Building Another One (Bootstrapped Founder transcript)
sources.summary: Tibo explains why he sold two platform-dependent SaaS products, how revenue tripled after the sale by shipping more and running yearly challenges, and why lean teams, DM-based support and shipping messy content work. He also covers buying Typeframe with a revenue-share deal and managing AI and platform risk.

principles.text: Ship more across features, SEO and social. Most experiments fade, but a few win big.
principles.quote: My strategy right now with Tom is do a lot. I really do more, ship more in terms of feature, SEO contents, social media contents. And the thing is a lot of those are fading, but a few of them are succeeding in very big ways.

principles.text: Recurring annual campaigns tied to user motivation (like New Year growth challenges) can become a reliable acquisition engine.
principles.quote: for every new year, just tell themselves this year is going to be the year where I'm going to be serious about Twitter or serious about LinkedIn. And we are trying to help them like motivate them on a daily basis

principles.text: Keep the team lean so you can go from idea to live without layers of approval.
principles.quote: we have always remained very lean with the team. And I think that's a part of what makes us go very fast.

principles.text: As a small founder, be directly reachable. Fast fixes from real-time DM support impress users and improve the product.
principles.quote: we're redirecting people to my own Twitter DMS. And so I got the DM in real time ... I was able to listen, see a feedback and try to implement the fix in like five minutes.

principles.text: Start with messy content and ship consistently. Quantity leads to quality, and you improve by living with the shame of shipping.
principles.quote: I'm a big believer of like, quantity leads to quality

principles.text: Buy stalled products with a revenue-share deal, then convert them to subscriptions to grow fast.
principles.quote: I switched it to a subscription based products. And from September to December, we went from zero to 4k in monthly recurring revenue.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo walks through the repeatable 12-step process behind four SaaS apps passing $100K MRR. The core idea: ship MVPs in days, talk daily to relevant users until retention is sticky, then go broad on distribution and double down on one or two channels. He also explains why he runs a portfolio of products.

chunks.heading: Build the MVP in days or weeks, not months
chunks.text:
- Tibo says to use shortcuts: no-code (he built some MVPs on Bubble.io) and boilerplates. He accepts skipping things that expert developers refuse to compromise on.
- His reasoning is the failure rate: "You will have a 90% failure rate." At one year per attempt, finding a winner could take 9 years.
- He compresses the cycle so he can ship a new project every week and reach success much faster.

chunks.heading: Find 5-10 truly relevant users and build a relationship
chunks.text:
- After the MVP, he finds five to ten people who are the core target audience, reaching out by tweet, subreddit or email.
- Relevance is the point. If the tester is not in the target audience (his example: your mom), the feedback, positive or negative, teaches nothing.
- He then builds a real relationship with each person to understand their life, their pain and their workflow, so the product delivers real value.

chunks.heading: Talk to users every day and be the user yourself
chunks.text:
- He wants recurring usage, so he talks to users daily to learn why they come back or don't, then reproduces that for others.
- Until a product reaches 10K/month in revenue, the support link in each product points to his Twitter DMs. This creates a daily flow of users and makes them feel close to him.
- Fixing something in 5 to 10 minutes can turn that person into a customer for life. Shipping a requested feature within an hour or two makes the user an advocate who talks about the product.
- He uses his own products, which makes him "10 times more relevant" on the core problem. Any tiny thing to fix, he just fixes.
- He states the core job as understanding the user's core need: keep a constant communication channel (social works well) and use your own product.

chunks.heading: Understand the user's ultimate goal, then iterate until they can't live without it
chunks.text:
- Knowing how far you can help users reach their ultimate goal lets you generate 10x or 100x more value.
- Build features that solve users' problems, not your own.
- Repeat the talk-build-fix loop while staying active on social media, where he sees new requests daily.
- He warns against going to acquisition too early. With low retention, you spend energy pushing people in and "99% of those people are going to flow away."
- Complaints are a good sign: a user who takes time to complain is committed and wants you to fix it.

chunks.heading: Distribution: go broad, then become a media company
chunks.text:
- Once stickiness exists, he tries many acquisition channels to see which work for that product.
- Launching on Product Hunt and talking about the product on social (building in public) is free. For him it is the default until 10K of revenue and is enough to reach the 1-3K/month needed to live and reinvest.
- At some point a company must become a media company: pick socials, SEO or cold email and build a content pipeline.
- That means having something to say about your industry, testimonials and case studies of very successful users, and an engine that fuels everything else.

chunks.heading: Scale with sustainable channels, then concentrate
chunks.text:
- For scaling he picks SEO, ads and affiliation, because you can set them once and scale to high limits. If ads work at 1K/month budget, they can often go to 10K or 100K with ongoing optimization.
- Example: Outrank grew from 0 to 20K/month by building in public. To keep the rhythm past 20K they started ads, invested in SEO with a dedicated hire, and ramped the affiliate program by making recommending Outrank easy. That took it from 20 to 200.
- Step 12 is to scale what works and kill what doesn't. Though he goes broad earlier, growth for each product comes from one or two channels, and he goes all in on those. Once SEO works, there is endless SEO work: new keywords and queries.

chunks.heading: Portfolio strategy and his products
chunks.text:
- Reported portfolio: Rabbit.ai (video making, about 400K/month, growing about 10% month over month), Alfronk (blog generator becoming an all-in-one SEO tool, just passed 200K/month), Super X (X audience tool, 13K/month), Post Sinker (posts to 10 platforms, 1.5K/month), and Feather (Notion-to-blog tool, about 10K/month, acquired for 250K).
- Combined: about 700K/month, 50K paying customers, growing about 20% monthly for over 6 months.
- He runs multiple products for resilience, driven by fear: he has a wife and two kids and AI moves fast. If OpenAI kills one product, it is not the end of the world.
- He cites X's takeover almost killing Tweet Hunter while it made 200K/month.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo explains how he runs five AI businesses with a tiny team: validate with revenue from day one, ship many cheap experiments, stay in constant contact with users, and follow unexpected usage into pivots (product videos to Rabbit). He covers pricing at $50-100/month, churn thresholds, tool-based SEO, and building with AI in Cursor.

chunks.heading: Tibo's bar for validation: charge from day one, judge by revenue and churn
chunks.text:
- Tibo says the most common founder mistake is wanting to "not be wrong" more than wanting to succeed. People then force-sell instead of validating, and stop listening to signals pointing at a bigger opportunity.
- He charges from day one. His reasoning: "if there is no revenue, there's no stickiness in the revenue, it's going to be very hard to build a successful business." Tiny validation moments make it easy to lie to yourself.
- A decade ago, after college, he cared more about sounding important ("managing a team of 10", "raised 200k") than about a foundation of real revenue. He now relies on revenue only, to avoid spending 2 years on a product that ends with nothing.
- Churn bar: monthly churn better than 20% is worth pursuing. At 40%, a subscriber stays about two months, and the product is not sticky.
- He cites "max MRR": churn and acquisition together cap your revenue on an S-curve, and a high-churn product needs unsustainable acquisition to grow. He prefers to pivot and iterate until churn is under 20% before thinking about acquisition.
- He picks 20% because AI users hop between products; he says five years ago the bar would have been under 5%.

chunks.heading: Pivoting Typeframe into Rabbit (AI shorts)
chunks.text:
- Tibo acquired Typeframe (product videos) at about $1-2k/month. Making product videos is something people rarely do, so churn was high.
- He talked to users constantly and saw they were using it for something else. His rule: "When you have a product that is made for one thing and people are actually twisting it to turn into this other thing, that's usually a very strong signal that you have to follow."
- In 2024, AI video models only produced 5-second clips. Rabbit splits a long video into scenes and stitches many 5-second clips together, keeping characters and environments consistent. That stitching is still the core engine.
- He pivoted completely: rebranded, bought a new domain, relaunched.
- Rabbit now offers more than 100 tools, including music videos (drop a Spotify link or audio file, choose a character), YouTube-to-shorts, avatars, and an auto mode that turns new blog posts or channel content into videos automatically.
- It does a bit over $600k/month with a team of about four. Each new AI video model release made it take off again.
- He thinks the product video idea alone could have reached roughly $10k/month, but pivoting gave him another shot at something bigger. Pivoting several times gave him multiple shots at winning.
- When he pivots, he refunds existing customers, locks them out, and does not let them block the decision.

chunks.heading: Keeping a direct feedback line with users
chunks.text:
- Tibo says the one thing needed to understand a product's core problem is constant communication with users.
- With Tweet Hunter, his first successful product, the in-app support button sent users to his Twitter DMs. It was overwhelming, but as the builder he heard every bug, pain point and feature request.
- He did the same with Typeframe.
- Today Rabbit and Outrank are big enough that he has hired customer support. He still gets DMs and likes them because they keep him "inside the loop".

chunks.heading: Ideas, quantity over quality, and shipping fast
chunks.text:
- Idea source: look at products you already pay for and build a more specific version that fits your own, narrower use case. Other people likely share your odd situation.
- He suggests copying an existing (often expensive) SaaS and niching down. He thinks $10k/month is already a huge success and enough to be "completely free, no boss", and says hitting $1M/month is very hard and he never expected it.
- Before his earlier project was acquired, he spent about four months shipping one new product per week: build a landing page, tweet it, check traction. If none, move on; if traction, build the product and onboard sign-ups. "Nine products failed... and the 10th one just took off."
- He now believes quantity leads to quality. The best product in a series of many tends to be better than one built with sole focus on quality. He recalls a Harvard-style experiment where a class split into one-essay and ten-essay groups produced the best essays from the quantity group.
- He says he cannot predict his winners; his successful products surprised him. He treats every release as an experiment that can fail.
- He builds many small single-page tools (e.g. an AI Reddit humanizer, a tweet rewrite and validation tool) to test whether people use them, to start ranking, and to start user conversations.
- An audience gives a shot but does not make an unsuccessful product succeed. You can hack your way to $5-10k/month, but going beyond needs a sustainable channel.

chunks.heading: SEO playbook: domain rating plus tools
chunks.text:
- SEO is his favorite channel and the number one acquisition channel for Rabbit, because it gives a recurring flow of interested users. He says "tons of people are calling SEO to be totally dead. It's really not the case for me."
- Two components:
  - Domain rating: it is very hard to rank with a new domain under about 20 DR. Outrank's backlink exchange marketplace helps raise it cheaply. Ranking in search also matters for being mentioned by ChatGPT.
  - Tools: Google's AI snippets make blog posts harder to rank, but cannot replace tools. Rabbit has a dedicated page per tool (e.g. audio to video).
- Keyword research: type phrases like "AI video tools for" into Google and treat every suggestion as a candidate landing page. He gives Peter Levels' Photo AI as an example of a famous founder still building many specific landing pages for SEO.
- Domain relevance matters. Competitors with "AI video" domains rank more easily, so he gave up on "AI video" and targets niche keywords.
- AI makes spinning up many landing pages easy, which makes differentiation harder. He says ranking now needs strong content, instant load speed and backlinks.
- Tool: Ahrefs. He says it is expensive but worth it.

chunks.heading: Outrank and the portfolio
chunks.text:
- Outrank started as a tool that publishes blog posts daily and evolved into a full SEO solution with the backlink exchange marketplace. He says it might reach $1M/month on its own.
- His five products are all AI-related. Super X crossed $30k/month. He keeps small projects because they could outgrow the biggest ones, as has happened before. He compares it to a diversified portfolio.
- He doesn't see himself going from five projects to 20, and is trying to remove himself as a bottleneck.

chunks.heading: Landing pages, pricing and running lean with AI
chunks.text:
- Landing page purpose: move visitors from a visit to a sign-up. Social proof is the most important element given trust issues in AI: testimonials, user counts, numbers. For Outrank he built success stories from real users with large business impact.
- He says most people jump to the product too soon. Describing the problem and why it is hard to solve is forgotten but important.
- Pricing: he picks ideas where he can charge about $50-100/month and adapts the product and AI usage to fit. At that range people don't ask for quotes before subscribing, and customers are higher quality with lower churn. At $20 or $9 you get churn, refund requests and the position of a cheap product; he wants to be the premium product.
- Team: he uses contractors and keeps the team very lean. He is "convinced right now that just one person can do the job of 20 compared to like 5 years ago." In the past he had a 20-person team for one product and says convincing each person of a new direction when pivoting is exhausting.
- Tooling: Cursor, with GPT 5.4 for complex non-UI work and Gemini 3.1 Pro for UI. He says the model mix changed within two weeks (Opus was his favorite before). One prompt in Cursor with Gemini 3.1 Pro produced a landing page animation.
- Spec workflow: he talks with the AI in Cursor to generate a spec, discards about 50% of them and restarts rather than editing, and repeats until he'd use the feature. To visualize a spec, he asks the AI for an image prompt and runs it in Google's Nano Banana 2 to get a dashboard mockup.
- Building is no longer the bottleneck: his backlog is empty and small items take about 10 minutes. The hard parts are good ideas and earning trust and promotion.
- Support automation: if he does something twice, he automates it. He uses text shortcuts (e.g. a refund macro that forwards to the right teammate) and has hired support for the larger products.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo explains how he and his co-founder shipped about 10 products in four months, hit on Tweet Hunter, then used creator equity partnerships and free SEO mini tools to grow Taplio. He also covers building for yourself, an earn-out heavy acquisition, and the LinkedIn ban.

chunks.heading: Building products for himself first
chunks.text:
- Tibo argues that building for your own problems is a big advantage: "you are such an expert at understanding your own problems that it makes the building so easier."
- He built Tweet Hunter for himself because he struggled to grow an audience on Twitter. He used the product daily to post and find inspiration.
- Every small annoyance sent him back to the code. That "never ending loop of fixing stuff" is why the product reached "super super high quality."
- He says his failed ideas were not for him. One example was a search engine for communities where founders could find places to promote their product. He now sees it as a bad idea for two reasons:
  - Users would launch once, so there is no recurring use.
  - Dropping a product into a community and leaving doesn't work. People ban you, or you get no results.
- He still says he had to build it to learn why it wouldn't work.

chunks.heading: Shipping a product a week to find one that works
chunks.text:
- After two startups that each took about two years to fail, Tibo and co-founder Tom decided to succeed or fail fast.
- They shipped a new product every week. If it brought no revenue within a few weeks, they moved on.
- They shipped roughly 10 products over four months, building a small audience and learning what people want along the way.
- Tweet Hunter was the 8th product, and it took off from the start.

chunks.heading: How Tweet Hunter went viral
chunks.text:
- It launched around the GPT-3 rush. Most people used GPT-3 to generate tweets, but it wasn't good enough for that.
- Tibo and Tom used it to analyze, cluster and categorize old viral tweets instead. This became the "inspiration wall," Tweet Hunter's core feature: evergreen viral tweets users could draw ideas from.
- Early promotion was Twitter posts and a few Reddit posts.
- Even after they stopped talking about it, new subscribers kept arriving, which told them they had a viral product.
- Tibo's view: a product aimed at people active on social media is organic by nature. If users succeed with it, they talk about it. So "work more on the product and a little bit less on the distribution."

chunks.heading: Equity partnerships with creators
chunks.text:
- Tibo cold-reached big Twitter accounts. One, with about 40K followers who was growing fast and talked about the same topic as Tweet Hunter, reacted enthusiastically and wanted to become a shareholder.
- They gave him 25% of Tweet Hunter, and it "worked so well."
- For Tapio (the LinkedIn product), they spent about six months looking for the right LinkedIn influencer. This was the longest part. The product was nearly ready before they found him. They partnered with Alex Burman.
- They targeted LinkedIn because its users have more money, are more willing to buy, and include salespeople who buy quickly.
- Tibo thinks builders and makers "do not partner enough with influencers and creators." Many big creators don't make much money and would happily partner with talented builders.
- With one distribution person and one builder, he says, that is "way enough to build the business."

chunks.heading: Mini free tools as an SEO acquisition channel
chunks.text:
- Tapio's biggest acquisition channel became free mini tools that rank on Google. Each is a landing page with one specific goal, such as downloading a video from a LinkedIn post.
- The tool does the job, then suggests using Tapio (for example, to schedule that video).
- They shipped about one new mini tool every month or two weeks. Today, he says, one can be built in a day or two.
- The video downloader began as a developer's hiring test. It was good enough that they hired the developer and published the tool.
- Social media was the first channel at the start. Mini tools later took over because their traffic compounds. Each new tool doesn't hurt the others, whereas a creator partnership or viral post "is a spike and then it goes to zero."
- Tapio combined both: being active themselves, sponsoring many creators, and building searchable tools.
- He thinks people are leaving SEO "way too soon." It still feeds most of his projects, so he invests in SEO tools.

chunks.heading: The earn-out acquisition and growth after
chunks.text:
- At sale, the company was about a year old, with two products (Tweet Center for Twitter and Tapio for LinkedIn). Elon Musk was taking over Twitter, and Tapio wasn't fully compliant with LinkedIn, so it was a risky deal.
- The deal was structured with about 80% as earn-outs tied to growth milestones and 20% upfront, which de-risked the sale for them.
- The original plan was to build, reach 10K monthly revenue, sell for 1 million and start over.
- Early buyers in India and the US wanted them to stay two years, which they feared. They sold to a former middle-school classmate who founded Lamb List and Lempire. He had been Tapio's first big client, buying 17 licenses for his team.
- Sale in summer 2022: annual revenue was a little under 1.5 million, about 75% Tweet Hunter and 25% Tapio.
- By April 2024, annual revenue was 8 million, with Tapio now about two thirds and Tweet Hunter one third.
- They hit five of six earn-out milestones and received 8 million of a possible 10 million.
- Enterprise sales were a gap. He and Tom dislike calls and custom onboarding, and limited support, so they only scratched the surface of B2B selling. He sees room in turning LinkedIn followers into clients and using LinkedIn data as purchase intent.

chunks.heading: The LinkedIn ban
chunks.text:
- Tapio's analytics and a large database of LinkedIn posts for the inspiration feature relied on a Chrome extension using LinkedIn's internal API.
- That broke LinkedIn's rules. It was safe for users but not for Tapio, and LinkedIn suspended his account about two years after Tapio's creation. By then he had been out of the business for about six months.
- The ban was about the extension, not AI content creation itself.

chunks.heading: His current challenge
chunks.text:
- After leaving in April 2024, Tibo returned to builder mode with a challenge: build five products to 100K monthly revenue each.
- The most successful so far is Revid AI, which turns text into video, aimed at TikTokers and YouTubers. He made a 5-minute explainer for his daughter on how a camera works.
- He shares wins and failures weekly at tmaker.io.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo Louis-Lucas explains how a steady stream of free SEO mini tools drove most of Tapo and Tweet Hunter's traffic. He covers the Vidio-style pattern of tools that drop users straight into the main product, why tool searches should survive AI search, and why "no AI" positioning is an uncrowded arbitrage. He also pitches a brand-sponsorship page business built on moderation.

chunks.heading: Free SEO mini tools as the main acquisition engine
chunks.text:
- Tibo built mini tools for Taplio and Tweet Hunter. Taplio is an AI-assisted LinkedIn scheduling and management tool.
- Content on Twitter and LinkedIn was everything at first. Then it "was just not enough".
- The team shipped "more than one per month" and ended with about 40 SEO-optimized mini tools.
- Together those tools brought roughly 70% of traffic.
- Each free tool ranks for many long-tail keywords. Visitors then discover and buy the main product.
- Tibo's test question: what free tool can I create that generates top-of-funnel traffic, where people who use it are naturally the buyers of my product?
- Best performer: "download video from LinkedIn post", a low-intent keyword for Taplio but about a million visitors a month. It ranked first.
- That tool was an evening's idea, built without even telling his co-founder. It was also the task they gave a developer they wanted to hire.
- Well-researched tools did not perform. His takeaway: "we know nothing basically", so ship many and see which wins.
- Result: downloaders are content creators, so the CTA was "schedule this on Taplio" or "on Tweet Hunter".

chunks.heading: Mini tools as features of the main product (the Vid.io pattern)
chunks.text:
- Tibo cites Vid.io, a video editor, as inspiration. It has around 50 tools such as crop video and compress video.
- Each tool takes your file as input, then redirects you into the main editor with the file already loaded. You are inside the product with no signup and no payment.
- Why it is cost-efficient: a new tool is just a feature of the main product, so it is cheap to build.
- Why it converts: users get a taste of the editor and think of it next time they need one.
- Tibo says he now runs Revid.ai, a video editor for short-form videos.

chunks.heading: Why tool-based SEO survives AI search
chunks.text:
- Tibo argues that "Google is dying because of GPT" matters less for action-based queries.
- Someone who wants to compress a video or download a LinkedIn video is looking for a tool. They are unlikely to ask ChatGPT and will search Google and click through.
- So he would "double down" on the mini-tool strategy.
- He is skeptical that tools get embedded in chat answers soon. Plugins and custom GPTs, in his words, "seem to be a failure", with only small use cases.
- On the host's view that LLMs will embed tools: Tibo accepts that Google now has more incentive to improve user experience, but is unsure.
