chunks.heading: Reddit and Quora answers as an LLM-visibility play
chunks.text:
- Tibo would invest heavily in answering Quora and Reddit questions, because LLMs likely draw answers from them.
- Example: to be the answer to "best sushi restaurant in Paris", get your pick to the top-voted Reddit answer.
- He believes AI plus proper context and instructions could eventually produce human-sounding replies, with a human touch, emotion and even errors. He sees it as a cat-and-mouse game between LLMs and content.
- He mentions Peter Levels blocking anyone he suspects of AI replies, and wonders about the error rate.

chunks.heading: Anti-AI positioning as an arbitrage
chunks.text:
- Tibo is working on SuperX, a Chrome extension for X with strong analytics. Adding AI replies would label it a gray-hat tool that makes Twitter worse with "shitty contents".
- He is therefore considering an anti-AI positioning.
- Idea: a suite of tools with no AI that people are happy to promote, because promoting them signals they are genuine humans.
- His competition argument: AI is brutally crowded, with "10 competitors" jumping on any AI idea. Levels and Danny Postma said their next product will be a no-AI product. Anti-AI has far fewer competitors.
- He points to 37signals / Basecamp (Jason Fried) as likely to keep making no-AI products, and wants to see their next one.
- He calls anti-positioning "so underrated" because it stands out when everything else looks the same.

chunks.heading: Brand and creator sponsorship marketplace ideas
chunks.text:
- Tibo thought the brand-influencer matching space was dead and saturated until he noticed Passionfruit. It offers creators ready-to-book sponsorship packages (tweet, YouTube video) with payment and calendar. Brands book with no signup via an email flow.
- His lesson: when you think a space is saturated, "you can just do 100 more things".
- Idea: flip it for brands, with a link-tree-style page where brands list the sponsorships they want and creators apply.
- Evidence: Tweet Hunter opened such a page for Twitter creators. It showed a rough calculation of payment and asked creators to plug in their Twitter handle and apply. Applications arrived by email and the team started the conversation there.
- Result: hundreds of applications after one tweet, which became "a nightmare to sort". Moderation and sorting is the real problem to solve.
- Product: AI to sort, grade and moderate inbound creators, and handle the back-and-forth of guidelines and validation.
- Pricing: charge for moderation and booking handling. Alternatively take a cut of sponsorships or sell a subscription by brand size, but not at the very beginning.
- Getting brands: scrape brands currently sponsoring creators. Keywords like "sponsored by" or "together with" appear in most sponsorship posts and newsletters. Reach out to them with this.
- SEO tool angle: build a free, SEO-optimized library of past sponsorships that worked, with pages per niche (e-commerce, AI, coaching). Rank for long-tail keywords, then sell the main product.
- Link-tree-style products generate static pages for clients. With custom domains, linking back to the main product builds backlinks fast.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo explains his shift from ego-driven, VC-funded failures to building revenue-first products. He covers the equity-for-influencer launch that took Tweet Hunter from 3K to 20K MRR in two weeks and his co-maker model of rescuing stuck products with distribution. He also shares retention lessons from Outrank and what he'd change in an exit.

chunks.heading: Why the failures stopped: build for revenue, not for the family dinner
chunks.text:
- Tibo failed for about four years. His diagnosis: he was "doing everything I could to just feel good at a family dinner to boost my ego" (managing 20 people, raising VC money), with no clients and no real traction behind it.
- The shift came in 2021: no employees, no VC, just him and his co-founder, aiming for a decent revenue and a good living rather than "the next Facebook".
- He frames it as building for yourself (to make money and be free) rather than to prove something to others.
- He and his co-founder (a marketing person he met in business school) set a challenge to create and ship one new product per week until one stuck. Eight or nine went nowhere; Tweet Hunter was the 11th and took off fast.
- His build habit: when he has an idea he doesn't discuss it, he builds a prototype in 6 to 8 hours and sends it to his co-founder. If the co-founder doesn't see it at first, he iterates a few days and shows it again.

chunks.heading: Tweet Hunter: scratch your own itch, ship one feature
chunks.text:
- Twitter had been the acquisition channel for his first user on nearly every product, so he wanted to grow an audience there himself.
- He downloaded viral tweets, used early GPT-3 to categorize and cluster them (e.g. startup-related or not), and browsed them in a CLI to spark his own content. Posting from that worked, so he turned it into a product.
- The MVP was one feature: a search bar returning viral tweets on a topic (e.g. "marketing") for inspiration. Behind it sat the AI clustering algorithm. It launched on Twitter and Reddit like that.
- His lesson: "by doing something for myself first, I was able to build something useful which then became a product."
- Later he built a Twitter scheduler out of the inspiration feature.

chunks.heading: The GK Moreno partnership: giving equity to a distribution partner
chunks.text:
- At about $1-2K MRR, he reached out to big influencers somewhat randomly. GK Moreno replied "okay I want in": the product matched the methodology of his Twitter course, and he wanted to be a co-founder, not just promote it.
- Deal: GK Moreno got up to 25% of the product. Tibo calls 25% of a small team "quite big", but says it worked incredibly well. Complication: he already had a marketing co-founder, so they worked out an agreement.
- They worked in "staff mode" for about two months, improving the product.
- GK's own launch in September 2021 took them from $3K to $20K MRR in about two weeks.
- He expected heavy churn after the launch; it didn't happen. They then grew about 20% month over month, from roughly $20K to $200K/month over a year and a half.
- Tibo later replicated the influencer-maker model on every new product, but now he is the creator and partners with a developer.

chunks.heading: The influencer flywheel and why he dropped it
chunks.text:
- For Taplio they replicated the approach: a LinkedIn influencer partner, plus a group of about 15 Twitter influencers each getting 0.1% of profits and 0.1% of the exit.
- To make "yes" easy, there was no obligation: they'd love shares and feedback, but the contract required nothing. About 80% of those approached said yes, even though Tweet Hunter was only around $30K/month then.
- Each launch or feature announcement then got amplified by 15 high-caliber influencers.
- He hasn't repeated the group: profit payouts and exits are hard to organize and sustain, and he says crypto/NFT tooling that could have handled it now "screams scam".

chunks.heading: Marketing: sell the outcome, not the feature
chunks.text:
- Tweet Hunter's first positioning was feature-level: inspiration to write better tweets. He moved up the chain: better content, more followers, a better personal brand, a more successful business, more money.
- Changing the marketing to that outcome "worked like 10 times more". He applies it to all new products.

chunks.heading: Co-maker model: take over stalled products and fix retention
chunks.text:
- How he finds partners: posting on X, and since the exits, inbound DMs from builders. If a product is well built, he proposes working together.
- His framework: find someone with an interesting idea and decent execution, stuck at $200-300/month without knowing how to escape. Revamp core things, work with 10 to 20 users for weeks or months to learn what makes it sticky and distinctive, then go broad using his audience, newsletter, SEO and ads knowledge.
- Why it beats hiring a developer for your own idea: on their own project the dev stays highly motivated.
- The big lever is talking to users. Until $10K MRR, the in-app support button on his products goes to his X DMs. The goal is to understand the user's core workflow and why the product does or doesn't fit it, not to fix color requests.
- Hundreds of tiny things (design, conversion rates, onboarding) also matter, and he says the bar rises because AI makes products better: "you have to raise your standards."

chunks.heading: Outrank: forcing stickiness with auto-publishing
chunks.text:
- Outrank began as a blog post generator (input a topic, edit, publish). It was well built but gave users no reason to return, since people lack the discipline to come back daily.
- Fix: make the software do the work automatically every day. It understands the product, researches competitors, generates high-volume low-difficulty keywords, and publishes one post per day to the user's CMS. Users can review beforehand, but "if you don't, it's going to be published anyway", which forces them to return and cut churn.
- It publishes daily on all his own five projects.
- Network effect: Outrank cross-links its users' sites to build authority. SaaS sites suit this; for niches like a bakery it's hard to find related users to link between.
- Outrank has crossed $200K/month. The Revid product earns slightly more; he doesn't share its numbers because the space is competitive.
- He attributes his recent success to combining dev skills, SEO and social distribution. He uses every product himself and sends the team constant feedback.

chunks.heading: Audience building, working style, and exit lessons
chunks.text:
- On X: consistency over talent. "I'm not the best writer", but he shows up daily, is nice to people and shares work. Even past 100K followers, some threads got two likes.
- Routine: works 9am to 5pm at his desk, takes no calls, keeps team communication written.
- Exit: Tweet Hunter and Taplio sold for $8M total, mostly earnout-based (about 25% upfront, 75% via revenue milestones over two years). Because they insisted on keeping control, he felt little buyer help on promotion and put heavy pressure on himself.
- His new rule: no exits. If he ever sells again, he'd insist on no earnout and a transition of 3 months max.
- Twitter API: after Musk's takeover the free API became $42K/month. They could afford it but were cut off for 48 hours while arranging payment.
- He started new products before his earnout ended, so he never had a break.
- Money: Peter Levels told him a steady revenue stream is healthier than one lump sum. Tibo spends only about what he earns monthly.
- Product advice: when you have an idea, build it in two days with AI and put it in front of relevant users rather than showing a piece of paper.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo recounts two failed startups, then a "fail in two weeks, not two years" approach: ship a product a week and judge only by revenue. That led to Tweet Hunter (the 11th product), built on his own problem and grown through building in public, SEO and an influencer partner, then sold on a 20% upfront / 80% milestone deal. He also covers owning your audience via newsletters, AI shifting value to distribution, and partnering with makers instead of hiring.

chunks.heading: Failing fast: Tibo's path from two failed startups to Tweet Hunter
chunks.text:
- Tibo's first startup was a kids' chores motivation app. He calls it a predictable failure: he and a few students were desperate for an idea and picked one that sounded great to everyone around them, but never got real market validation from users.
- His second was a kids' coding game, built as a video game to compete with other games for kids' attention. He raised about $400,000 and grew the team to 15-20 people (artists, game designers, front-end and back-end developers).
- That company had plenty of free players but no revenue. His verdict: "if people do not convert to paid user you don't have a real product like you don't have a real business."
- He reacted to the first failure by thinking he needed more money, a bigger team and a more ambitious project, and the second failure came from doing exactly that in an industry he knew almost nothing about.
- Total of roughly four years across the two failures, on a very low salary. He names that as his biggest sacrifice.
- His resolution afterward: "if we need to fail again it needs to be in two weeks and not in two years."

chunks.heading: Ship a product a week and judge only by revenue
chunks.text:
- Starting over, Tibo and his team shipped a new product roughly every week until one produced revenue. They did this for about four months.
- They looked at revenue only to decide whether a product worked, not vanity metrics like engagement or free users.
- Tweet Hunter was the 11th product shipped in that window and it took off from the start.
- Each product showed the same pattern: two acquisition channels brought most users, Reddit and Twitter. Reddit was hard to systemize with a repeatable recipe. Twitter had many things that could be automated and that worked again and again, so they built for Twitter.
- The path: first a GPT-3 tweet generator (didn't work well, GPT wasn't good enough then), then GPT-3 used to cluster and categorize content (worked "so so"), then Tweet Hunter, which resurfaces old viral tweets and repurposes them.
- He built Tweet Hunter for himself first and was its first user; it helped him grow a Twitter audience daily. He calls this founder-product fit.

chunks.heading: Build for your own problems
chunks.text:
- The main thing that works now and didn't before: becoming an expert in the problem he's solving, by solving his own problems.
- Earlier he solved problems he thought he understood, but "the degree of understanding that you have is very low level." You miss the deep core need of the audience because it's usually not what they tell you.
- His advice to new founders in 2025: the first idea will probably fail, but build it anyway so the second or third succeeds. To raise the odds, start by building something for yourself, since "building a good product is in the first place a true understanding of the problem that you are solving."

chunks.heading: Launching Tweet Hunter with an influencer co-founder
chunks.text:
- Tibo messaged many big names on Twitter to get them using Tweet Hunter. One was already teaching a course on the exact technique built into the product, loved it, and wanted to join as a co-founder.
- It wasn't the plan, but Tibo gave him up to 25% of the product and says he didn't regret it.
- They launched on Twitter in September 2021 using this partner's launch plan. In three weeks they went from $3K monthly revenue to well above that (the transcript cuts off the exact figure, "more thank").

chunks.heading: Growth levers: personal branding, SEO and building in public
chunks.text:
- Two levers drove a 7x rise: social media and personal branding, and SEO.
- On social: build in public, share how you grew, what you did, user stories and success stories.
- On SEO: constantly publish new pages and new tools that rank on Google. It compounds into more traffic over time. He thinks startups underrate SEO because talking about what you do on Twitter is trendy and getting saturated.
- Why build in public: tips you hold back will probably be shared by someone else, who gets the credit. Sharing tips and true numbers daily earns trust: people believe you ship quality products and treat customers well. That trust turns into feedback, purchases, promotion and people plugging your new product into their newsletters.
- He started Tweet Hunter with about 1,000 followers, 99% of them bots or dead accounts, and built his audience by sharing useful things daily. His audience came from sharing; Tweet Hunter didn't succeed because of an existing audience. He now has 130K+ on Twitter.
- He says the newer Twitter algorithm rewards interesting content rather than follower counts, so anyone can still get reach.
- LinkedIn: many salespeople, who buy quickly if you show value, and higher buying power with less scam and low-quality users than Twitter.
- Downside of personal branding: LinkedIn suspended his account over his involvement in Taplio (a LinkedIn tool built on a Chrome extension they can't fully control), even after he had left the product. He lost the account. Lesson: "you do not own your followers." What you do own is a newsletter subscriber base, which can be exported and sold.

chunks.heading: The acquisition: 20% upfront, 80% on revenue milestones
chunks.text:
- The original plan was to reach $10K per month and sell for about $1M. They grew far past that, to roughly $130K per month at sale.
- Buyers wanted founders to stay two years, because the business was risky: Elon Musk was changing Twitter's rules, and Taplio wasn't compliant with LinkedIn's rules.
- He chose a French buyer (about 50 people, same culture and language, whose founder was a former middle-school classmate and Tweet Hunter customer) over a US and an Indian company he knew nothing about.
- Deal structure: only 20% paid upfront, the other 80% unlocked via revenue milestones over two years. They hit five of six milestones, growing from $1.5M to $8M per year in under two years.
- The buyer gave them full independence, which helped execution but left few bridges between teams. He thinks tighter collaboration could have grown it more, though he wanted the freedom.
- In March 2023 Twitter raised its API price from zero to $42K per month and cut access within days. Tibo says most Twitter products died, and a few acquired Twitter tools strengthened Tweet Hunter's position. He notes the fee is a barrier for new entrants but manageable for products with revenue.

chunks.heading: Feather: buying a product and undercutting Beehiiv on price
chunks.text:
- Beehiiv emailed him a price rise of about 2.5x for his newsletter. His own price rises were typically 10% to 30%, and grandfathered existing users.
- He called them out on Twitter, got traction, and started wondering about building his own newsletter platform.
- He was already buying Feather (a blog platform that turns Notion docs into a blog), his biggest acquisition so far (he has done more than 10, mostly much smaller), for $250,000 of his personal money, "the biggest risk I ever took."
- He found another tool that sends newsletters from Notion, asked the founder to sell, and merged it into Feather. It took far longer than expected because sending newsletters is hard.
- Pricing difference: Beehiiv charges per subscriber (he cites about $250 per month at 1K+ followers, roughly $500 per month at his scale, and says he isn't sure of the exact figure). Feather charges about half that and is aimed at solopreneurs who send rarely. He sends a daily newsletter to about 137,000 people on Feather.
- Beehiiv locked him out after noticing he was testing his own newsletter feature against theirs. He had already exported his subscribers, and says he'd never use a platform that doesn't allow export.

chunks.heading: Ego, teams, and how he works with makers
chunks.text:
- Advice to his younger self: a big team looks good at a family dinner, but "that's ego feeding." What matters is selling: "people giving you money for your product is the ultimate validation that you are doing something useful."
- He has no employees. He runs four products, each partnered with one skilled maker who owns a share and manages themselves.
- He finds partners on Twitter, running several candidates in parallel with a paid two-week trial, and tells them honestly that several people are competing. He believes a real trial beats any interview.
- After the trial the partner gets equity or revenue share.
- His red-flag rule: a red flag never shrinks, it only grows, so pull back when you see one.
- Daily habit: tackle the hardest task first, start coding or writing with coffee, and get two hours of focused work with no distraction before email or DMs. His goal is to ship something each day that others can see or use.
- His view on AI: building costs are heading toward zero, so value shifts to distribution, storytelling and educating users. He uses Cursor daily for coding and expects AI-driven tools to catch security bugs in AI-written code.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo Louis-Lucas explains his revenue-first validation approach, shipping a product a week until one stuck, going deep on a single platform, and giving product-level equity to influencers for distribution. He also covers why he now avoids selling, uses DMs over calls, and runs five product-led SaaS solo with AI.

chunks.heading: Validation means revenue, not usage
chunks.text:
- Tibo lost two years each on a 2015 project and a 2017 project that were never validated. After the second, he and his co-founder set an absolute rule: "never ever again" work multiple years on a product that isn't validated.
- Number one mistake he sees: treating free users or usage as validation. His kids' programming game reached about 15k monthly users, but almost no paying users.
- Revenue (willingness to pay) is the signal. In 2021 the plan became shipping one new product a week until something stuck.
- Most of those products made roughly $200-300 a month. Tweet Hunter, the 11th product, hit $1k MRR in its first 2 weeks because "people were willing to pay just for the promise of what it was doing."
- Free users dominate feedback and skew the roadmap. In Outrank and Revid he has only paid users, so all feedback comes from people who pay, which he says makes implementation easier and higher quality.

chunks.heading: Going deep on one platform to beat saturated markets
chunks.text:
- Tweet Hunter entered a crowded scheduler market (Buffer, Hootsuite, Later), whose tools targeted enterprises and supported every social platform shallowly.
- Tibo integrated only Twitter, but at full depth: every Twitter feature, plus automations and integrations only possible with that focus.
- He targeted individual creators (the creator economy was starting in 2020-2021) rather than companies. An individual can realistically perform on one platform, so the depth-first tool became the obvious choice.
- He replicated this for LinkedIn with Taplio, as a separate product instead of folding it into Tweet Hunter. Reasons: supporting a platform deeply is hard across multiple channels, and the distribution model was tied to one platform's audience.

chunks.heading: Distribution share for influencers
chunks.text:
- On Tweet Hunter he gave 25% of the product to a Twitter influencer who ran all distribution. This was a product-level contract, not company equity: 25% of monthly profits plus 25% of any exit.
- The influencer's audience and methodology matched the product, so alignment was strong. He repeated it with a LinkedIn influencer for Taplio.
- He also created a group of up to 17 influential Twitter people, each owning 0.1% of the product, called the "creator investors."
- The contract placed no obligation to promote; they kept their share regardless. A few never promoted, but about 80% did, retweeting and sharing product updates.
- Tactic: treat them as investors, not affiliates. He sent monthly financial investor updates with key details, which was unusual for them and worked.

chunks.heading: Exits and earnouts
chunks.text:
- Tweet Hunter and Taplio sold together for $8 million (per the intro). Tibo says the churn, stakes and platform dependency (Twitter chaos in 2022, LinkedIn cracking down on non-compliant API use) forced a roughly 2-year stay and about 75% of the price as earnout.
- Earnout milestones turned the mood from gaining with each milestone to fearing losses if missed. He didn't enjoy it, so his new rule is "never sell ever again."

chunks.heading: Building the "indie hacker stack" portfolio
chunks.text:
- He runs five public products (plus a few in stealth), with a goal of a bootstrapped portfolio; he says they recently crossed $1M per month in payouts across the five.
- Strategy: pick a target persona (indie hackers, solo founders, tiny teams) and build everything they need to run a business, instead of picking an industry like video editing and building every tool for it.
- Portfolio is opportunity-driven, not a master plan. Outrank came from a founder whose product Tibo loved but saw big gaps in. After sharing lots of feedback they partnered as equals, with Tibo providing distribution.
- His best and worst performing products were both acquisitions, so he stays undecided on buy versus build.
- Each product has a different co-founder, and separate brands keep that fair. A personal brand across all of them would benefit him but not the partners.
- He considers product-led growth the only model: a product that isn't product-led "feels like a scam" because the product isn't good enough to drive growth.

chunks.heading: Shipping often and talking to users by DM
chunks.text:
- He expects a 5-10% success rate on new products (citing Peter Levels) and says more shipping is the way to learn what people want.
- Five years of daily posting on X toughened him to rejection, so "your product sucks" no longer hurts.
- He shifted from launch announcements to DM conversations with people actually trying the product: onboarding them, asking about pain, value and workflow. New products now go more into stealth with real users.
- He keeps a strict no-call policy to protect coding and family time; this podcast was his only call that week.

chunks.heading: AI-run operations and daily workflow
chunks.text:
- With AI he codes 0% himself and acts as QA. His backlog of ideas is now empty and he struggles to feed it, and the risk is feature creep, so he tries to build the right things but not too many.
- He keeps the stack he's most comfortable with; he says stack isn't a differentiator.
- Each morning he opens about 15 dashboards (Stripe, PostHog or Amplitude, ads, newsletter, social performance from his own tools Postsyncer and SuperX) in random order. Whatever grabs his attention (a spike, a dip, a viral tweet) sets that day's work: a campaign, an email, or a free lead-magnet product.
- He is moving off Claude Cowork-style chat to scheduled systems on Mission Control HQ (an OpenClaw wrapper). Example: a weekly job reads the last 7 days of Revid commits and emails affiliates a "what's new" digest so they promote more.
- Goal now: build systems so the portfolio scales beyond five products without him operating each one.

chunks.heading: Advice for product founders
chunks.text:
- Time AI spends working should go to customers, not TikTok or X. Spend it DMing people and understanding core needs.
- His method for resisting distraction: feeling guilty about it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo explains how, after two VC-funded failures, he and his co-founder shipped about one product a week until Tweet Hunter took off, then sold it with a revenue-linked earn-out. He covers building for your own pain, DM-driven support as marketing, influencer co-founders, free tools for SEO, and surviving platform risk.

chunks.heading: Why Tibo builds relentlessly for one audience and solves real problems
chunks.text:
- After two failed VC-backed startups, Tibo and his co-founder decided not to raise money and not to hire (they later had to change the hiring part).
- He says a big team without product-market fit is a nightmare to pivot: the team thinks you have no vision and loses motivation. He needed "two big failures" to learn this.
- At university in France, people tell you raising money and being "important" is the path. He did exactly that, right after graduating.
- New rule: "build relentlessly for the same people trying to solve the same problem." Everything built was meant to solve real problems, which he calls "10 times more sustainable."
- Ideas that sound good but come from problems you haven't worked on are usually bad businesses, because you lack history and core skills. You have to "get your hands dirty" to understand the user's core problem.

chunks.heading: Build for your own problem
chunks.text:
- Working on your own problems is "a huge competitive advantage."
- His first startup, an app to motivate kids to do chores, failed partly because he wasn't yet a parent and didn't understand the guilt and alone-time struggle.
- Tweet Hunter came from his own problem: he was trying to grow his Twitter audience, because Twitter was the best growth driver for all their products.
- If you build for yourself, you are the first customer, likely many others share the problem, and you know what is real value versus a useless nice-to-have.
- Whatever you do, you must do it for a long time. If it isn't a problem you care about, you'll give up after three months, which is too short to learn an industry's core problems.

chunks.heading: Shipping one product a week to find the winner
chunks.text:
- Previously they spent two years on one idea that got invalidated. This time they built roughly one new product per week and validated as fast as possible, moving on if it made no revenue.
- Over about three to four months this produced 11 products. Most made no revenue; per the transcript, some had users or modest cash flow, but nothing proved validation.
- Examples: Twitter analytics delivered by email, a community database and search engine for promoting products across Slack groups and Twitter accounts, and a GPT-3 tweet generator.
- The 11th was Tweet Hunter. From the first day of onboarding users, growth happened even without pushing it on Twitter.
- Original MVP: a huge categorized database of viral tweets. AI analyzed your account and surfaced viral tweets on your topic and in your style, shown as a wall of inspiration. The MVP was essentially one input field (e.g. "marketing").
- How to know when to stop: when it's not working you never know, but with true product-market fit "you know." He cites a YC-style idea that it is painful because users want it so badly it crashes your servers and overwhelms you.
- He thought in early 2021 they were too late for GPT-3 (a rival headline tool sold for $1M). He says that was wrong and that AI still has many opportunities.

chunks.heading: Support via Twitter DMs as a growth and product loop
chunks.text:
- The support button in Tweet Hunter pointed to his Twitter DMs. He kept Twitter and his code editor open all day, fixing things in real time.
- Because they used very flexible serverless tooling, a fix could ship about 5 to 10 minutes after the DM, and he'd reply "it's now fixed, you can see it in the app right now."
- Users tweeted about how fast the team was, which was a strong early marketing boost. It faded as the team grew and processes were added.
- Direct feedback loops beat quarterly NPS-style cycles at deciding what to build.

chunks.heading: Growth levers: influencer co-founder, tool credits, build in public, free tools
chunks.text:
- **Influencer CMO with equity:** a Twitter copywriter (around 4K followers then) asked for equity because Tweet Hunter's "wall of viral tweets" matched the copywriting method in his course. Tibo didn't want to give equity for a few promo posts, so the contract made him a real CMO who also had to run affiliates, SEO and ads, not just post.
- Goal then was only 10K MRR by end of 2021. They hit about 5x that in the first year.
- He ran a Twitter launch in September 2021 that took them from 3K to 20K MRR in three weeks.
- **Attribution by default:** early on, tweets showed the tool used to post them. Because the product was premium and attracted big viral accounts, "sent with Tweet Hunter" spread. Twitter later removed that.
- **Build in public:** sharing steps and learnings helped growth.
- **Free mini tools:** they built 20 to 30 free tools, each serving one need (e.g. analyzing your audience to find the best time to tweet). They are real apps with personalized answers, rank on Google for queries like "best time to tweet," and bring growing traffic.
- He argues Twitter and LinkedIn now drive B2B SaaS buying: people choose tools based on who they follow, and indie makers building in public gain an emotional audience relationship.

chunks.heading: Platform risk and moats on Twitter and LinkedIn
chunks.text:
- When Twitter moved API access from free to enterprise, the tier price they heard was $42,000 per month. Access was cut about four days after the announcement, so users couldn't post and other things broke.
- They worked frantically, built "crappy things" to bypass blockages, and coordinated with other Twitter-tool founders. After 48 hours, one of about 10 contacts replied and helped move them to the enterprise tier, which they now pay for.
- That contact came from a competitor. He distinguishes competitors who share contacts and help each other from those who tried to steal customers while they were nearly offline.
- On LinkedIn, the official API can't retrieve your posts, so no analytics. Taplio's workaround is a Chrome extension using LinkedIn's internal API, which is harder technically and explains why LinkedIn has far less competition than Twitter had.
- Taplio use case: export people who commented on your LinkedIn posts, find their emails and send them to lemlist, which is "almost warm emailing."
- On AI content, he thinks OpenAI's rules on social media use initially blocked this use case. His view is that people don't care if a tweet is AI-generated if it's good, and the best output is AI fine-tuned by humans. Good results need huge prompts that capture the user's tone and topics, which is the value the product adds.

chunks.heading: The exit: earn-out structure, timing and pick-the-right-industry advice
chunks.text:
- They sold with revenue a little below $2M annually. The deal could exceed $10M if revenue milestones are hit, structured with a large earn-out and six revenue milestones, so the upfront amount was "quite small." The goal is reaching $10M annual revenue.
- Earn-outs of around 50% over two years are common; one tied to massive growth is less so. The structure reflected how risky and platform-dependent the business was.
- Original plan was to sell at 10K MRR for a 10x multiple. He later realized going from 10K to 20K MRR is much easier than starting over, and valuation multiples improve at larger scale (about 100K MRR or more).
- Selling was hard: growth was strong and staying could have paid more, but the risk for two people was high.
- Advice: pick the right, fast-growing industry (they chose social media/creator tools plus AI) so you don't need crazy tech to grow. Don't hire early, build yourself, and build for yourself.
- He uses GPT-4 for most of his code: reusable prompts describing the project, stack and file hierarchy, then specific questions. He also argues serverless lets one person do what needed 10 to 20 people ten years ago.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo recounts how two failed early startups taught him to validate with payments, build hands-on, and ship fast. He then describes shipping one product a week until Tweet Hunter took off, and how a viral partner launch drove growth to an acquisition.

chunks.heading: Ship one product a week until something sticks
chunks.text:
- Tibo's early startups failed because he delegated the hard parts. After engineering school he had been told for five years that hands-on coding was a low-status job and that engineers should become project managers. So he hired a 10-15 person team of rotating junior interns and handed off the hardest tasks: building the product, understanding what people want, and marketing.
- He later reversed this: "being handsome" (hands-on, building himself) is enough, and with AI a very small team can now out-produce a 10-person team from 15 years ago.
- In 2020 he and his co-founder Toma started a "ship one new product every week until something sticks" experiment. In early 2021 they shipped roughly 10 or 11 projects in about four months.
- The weekly rhythm:
  - Build for a week.
  - The week after, announce on Twitter, collect feedback and talk to users.
  - While doing that, start the next product.
  - Keep what works and throw away what doesn't.
- Tweet Hunter came out of this loop and launched in early May 2021. He describes it as forcing opportunities instead of waiting for luck.

chunks.heading: Build for a problem you have, and use the product daily
chunks.text:
- Twitter was their main acquisition channel, and they wanted a bigger audience. Tibo started hacking together a database of viral tweets to learn which patterns worked, and that became the first Tweet Hunter product.
- Users entered a topic such as coding or SEO and got viral tweets on it, filtered toward their own writing style. GPT-3 was used to label, cluster and match tweets, not to generate content.
- He was the primary user, spending 30 to 60 minutes a day writing tweets with it, then fixing whatever annoyed him in the code. That daily use gave him both the deep problem understanding and a feel for tiny details like a misaligned button or a bad feedback effect.
- His advice: "You are basically an expert on your own problems." With today's market size, at least a thousand other people likely have the same problem.
- Fixing small things daily is what makes a product feel completely different.

chunks.heading: Validate with payments, not free usage
chunks.text:
- His first idea was an app that gamified motivation for kids' chores (brushing teeth, homework). It took two years to realize it wasn't working.
- The core mistake was that they never tried to validate the idea. They kept trying to sell it and convince people it was good.
- Structural problem: two clients (parents pay, kids must use it daily) and competition with every game on the kid's phone.
- Second mistake in both early startups: forcing adoption by going free first, "like Facebook," and finding the business model later. This only validates that people use something free.
- His current approach is the opposite: "The validation comes from the payments." He wants to prove people will pay, not just use.
- A good problem isn't enough. Habit and motivation content is hugely consumed, yet very few people act or pay.
- The product that works does what people want, not what the founder wishes the world worked like. He gives the example of startups built on the idea that people should want to meet strangers. You don't create new wants; you find existing needs and serve them in a new way.

chunks.heading: Influencer partnership and the growth curve
chunks.text:
- About two or three months after launch, Tibo did influencer outreach to people with 30K, 50K or 100K followers. One creator who taught people how to go viral on Twitter replied "I want to be in" after two or three DMs.
- The fit was strong because he taught the same method: building a swipe file of good viral content, which is what Tweet Hunter automates.
- They ran a joint launch that the partner handled entirely on Twitter. Monthly revenue went from 3K to 20K in September 2021.
- After that they grew about 20% month over month until reaching 100K-150K in monthly revenue.
- Behind the visible revenue chart was relentless daily work:
  - Adding features almost every day.
  - Shipping a free SEO tool almost every week to rank for keywords.
  - Talking to two or three people a day on Twitter to understand their pain points.
  - Fixing UI issues continuously.
- Tweet Hunter and its LinkedIn sister product Taplio were both acquired in 2022. Buyers required a two-year transition, so Tibo was free to start new projects only in 2024. He now works on four projects, one of which has taken off.

chunks.heading: Risk, failure and money
chunks.text:
- Tibo says he never saw startups as risky: he had no family to support, about 15,000 from his parents that he used over two years, and a working partner.
- The skills from failed startups paid off. After two failures he took a job paying about twice what 99% of his engineering-school peers earned, because he had hired a team, managed budgets and banks, and touched everything from front end to back end to server management.
- He admits the risk is genuinely higher for people with large salaries and family obligations.
- His parents' financial literacy shaped him. Today he faces a cash-flow squeeze: the payment provider pays him more than 30 days after a sale, but AI providers need payment immediately, so faster growth stretches cash further.
- His school gave him his co-founder. He thinks you can now find a strong first circle on X if you are consistent and motivated, and he now builds with people he hasn't met in person.

chunks.heading: Building in the AI era
chunks.text:
- He sees far more people shipping on X now (he estimates 10 to 20 times more), helped by the indie-hacker wave and AI lowering the skill bar.
- Copycats are common. After he talked publicly about a product (Revit) and how well it was working, an almost exact copy of the landing page and example videos appeared within a week. As a result he talks less about revenue on X than before.
- He tries not to judge whether this is good or bad and focuses on using the tools available to build the best products, noting there is a lot to build and it is much easier than before.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo Louis-Lucas explains how he shipped a product a week to find product-market fit, validated only by revenue, and sold Tweet Hunter and Taplio for about $8M. He covers a 25% profit-share deal with an influencer, free mini-tools for SEO, buying SaaS for distribution, and starting to build with AI.

chunks.heading: Validating ideas: revenue is the only signal
chunks.text:
- Tibo defines validation narrowly: "validation is about people paying for the product." Free users and people saying nice things don't count.
- His reasoning: people don't want to hurt your feelings, so they give positive feedback. If they aren't buying, you may not have product-market fit.
- Early on he raised VC money and built two failed startups. He wanted to avoid a third two-year failure, so he looked for ways to reach revenue fast.
- He charges from the start, even for betas. He gets angry comments such as "why should I pay for a beta?" and says that is part of the game; you ignore the haters.
- He rejected the idea that having a team signals success. His first startups had staff and VC money but no revenue. His current business is much more successful, yet he has a harder time explaining it to friends without saying "I have a team of 10."

chunks.heading: Shipping a product a week until one sticks
chunks.text:
- With his co-founder he shipped 11 products in about 11 weeks, one a week, to shorten the time to product-market fit. They kept going until something stuck, and Tweet Hunter was the one that did.
- It was not random. They picked one target (creators and solopreneurs) and one problem (how to sell your products/grow an audience).
- They were their own users, so they could tell whether each product was useful. Every launch also deepened their understanding of the audience and grew their following, so each later launch was easier.
- Tweet Hunter's path:
  - Tweet B: GPT-3 tweet generator. It didn't work because GPT-3 wasn't mature enough.
  - A tweet digest analytics email: about $300 monthly revenue, not enough.
  - Tweet Hunter: a wall of old viral tweets (3 to 6 months old), clustered and categorized with GPT-3, as an inspiration layer for writing. It worked from day one.
- Insight behind it: content recipes that worked before keep working, so you find a new way to talk about the same ideas.
- He now tries, at least once a week, to come up with an idea in the morning and ship it by end of day. This came from a daily "hackathon" group in Barcelona: introduce yourself at 9, work all day, demo at 4.
- His view: about 80% of what you ship won't work, but the 20% that does might never have been built otherwise. "Quantity beats quality" because you can't predict what takes off. He suggests carving out about 20% of your time for new shots.
- He cites that most A/B tests fail anyway, so more shots on goal beats heavy upfront planning.

chunks.heading: Influencer distribution deal: 25% of the product's profit
chunks.text:
- Tweet Hunter had a small following, so Tibo and his co-founder gave an influencer (JK) a distribution deal. In the transcript the share is described as 25%, and Tibo says they started at 30% ("not 25").
- Structure: it was a deal on the product, not the company. JK got 25% of monthly profit and 25% of any exit tied to that product. In return he owned marketing and had to actively promote it with campaigns and a referral program.
- They did the same for the LinkedIn product Taplio, scoping the deal to that product only, and found new partners for it.
- Results: they announced the partnership and launched together in September 2021. Monthly recurring revenue went from $3K to $20K in a few weeks. The goal for the whole year had been $10K, and they were at about $1K MRR when the talks began.
- Trust mechanics:
  - Full transparency: bank statements and Stripe access were shared.
  - Founders' salaries were not counted as costs.
  - The only way to manipulate profit would be to overpay contractors, which transparency made hard.
- His point: big influencers don't make as much money as people assume and want their own products. JK was around 21 and had no significant revenue, so the deal worked for both sides.
- For the exit, value was split by each product's revenue share. Tweet Hunter was about 80% of revenue; Taplio was 3 to 4 months old at the sale.

chunks.heading: Mini free tools as an SEO and backlink engine
chunks.text:
- Tibo launched many small, single-purpose free tools (tweet generator, bio generator, LinkedIn video downloader), each unbundled from a feature of the main product. Most launched on Product Hunt.
- Product Hunt gives a one-time spike, but the backlinks and Google rankings compound over time and become a long-term acquisition channel.
- Example: the Taplio LinkedIn video downloader generates about 1 million visits a month. He says it isn't closely tied to Taplio's main use case, but some visitors convert. It started as a test to evaluate a developer he was hiring. A developer built it, they shipped it, and about two months later it ranked first, with no launch and no strategy.
- He has shipped a tool in one or two days without telling anyone at least five times; sometimes one is an outlier. He credits being action-oriented and not weighing effort versus opportunity.
- He calls Product Hunt's maker of the year recognition a result of launching 10 to 15 times in a year, not of the two main products. He says he didn't capitalize on it.
- He is replicating this on every product, including his current project. He notes Vid.io-style variants are even easier: many "tools" that are just landing pages redirecting to one app with different entry points.

chunks.heading: Pricing, churn and trials
chunks.text:
- Taplio/Tweet Hunter monthly churn stayed between 10% and 15% for three years. He attributes it to a volatile audience: creators who decide to become a LinkedIn influencer, then switch to Instagram two weeks later.
- After three years he accepted churn couldn't be fixed and focused instead on activation and acquisition.
- Tibo went through about 10 price increases on Tweet Hunter. The biggest was 20 to 25%, and every one went well. They never lowered prices.
- Raising prices actually lowered churn, because it filtered out low-commitment, lower-quality users.
- He argues cutting price in half would need twice the subscribers or half the churn, which he doesn't think is achievable.
- They offered 7-day free trials with the credit card required up front.
- He was irritated by Beehiiv raising his price from $100 to $250 a month (2.5x for the same features), contrasting it with his own max of about 25% increases.

chunks.heading: Acquisition, earn-out and platform risk
chunks.text:
- Tweet Hunter and Taplio were sold to Lemlist in 2022 for up to $10M. Structure: about 10% upfront, about 80% as earn-outs over two years tied to six revenue milestones. They hit five of six and received about $8M.
- Reason for the structure: platform risk. The company was barely a year old, Elon Musk had just taken over Twitter, and Taplio wasn't fully compliant with LinkedIn rules.
- Post-sale, revenue grew from $1.5M to $8M ARR over two years with a team of about 7 growing to about 10 (3 or 4 developers) plus some agencies. Growth came from acquisition, not churn fixes. Tibo says Taplio drove growth for all of Lemlist while Lemlist was stagnating.
- They stayed independent: no meetings, no integration pressure, because they hit their goals. Tibo says an earn-out is not a relief: he worked "like crazy" for two years.
- Twitter API episode: Twitter announced the free API would become a $42K/month plan with 30 days notice, but cut access after 3 days of the Enterprise form being submitted. Few Twitter staff were reachable. Another tool-builder shared a key account manager's email, and that is how Tweet Hunter ended up paying $42K a month.
- LinkedIn: analytics aren't available via the API, so Taplio's Chrome extension reads them from the page HTML, which breaks LinkedIn's rules. About 6 months after leaving, Tibo's personal LinkedIn account was suspended. He says other tools do the same.

chunks.heading: Buying products, then forking and focusing on distribution
chunks.text:
- His thesis: the hardest part of startups is reaching product-market fit, so he buys small SaaS products that exist and focuses on growth.
- Typeframe (product videos) was bought for "tens of thousands." He forked it into Revid (short videos) and found a way to make it about 10x more profitable. He ran both for six months, then killed Typeframe and redirected its traffic to Revid. He says he did it a bit late and has never regretted killing a product.
- Feather (a Notion-to-blog tool) was bought for $250K. It grows slowly, has very low churn and is low maintenance.
- He then built newsletter features in Feather after the Beehiiv price rise. He ran 20% of his subscribers on Feather alongside 80% on Beehiiv to compare open and reply rates. Deliverability was much harder than expected. Beehiiv closed his accounts after his public criticism and what they called reverse engineering, so he moved fully to Feather.
- Worry and relief: when Notion launched Notion Sites in June he feared his $250K investment was worthless, but it increased attention on Notion-to-site tools.
- AI thesis: as AI makes software creation cost close to zero, the value shifts to distribution and integrations. He expects extremely niche software (for example a Notion for lawyers or accountants) and says distribution is "monetizable right away."

chunks.heading: Building in public and getting started with AI
chunks.text:
- Why build in public: it builds authority and personal attachment, and makes it easier to sell any product later. A small community gives feedback and buys early. Downside: copycats, who copy successful products and cut prices.
- He shares revenue milestones less now because it attracts copycats.
- Advice to non-coders (PMs):
  - Start a public account (Twitter/LinkedIn), document your goals and show progress daily, so social commitment creates pressure.
  - Use ChatGPT to learn Cursor, then build in Cursor with AI. Paste errors back to the AI.
  - Pick something fun, such as a project for your kid or a passion, because the first product probably won't work.
  - Don't spend hours on tutorials. Learning sticks when you hit the problem. Deploy on a platform like Vercel for free.
  - Show your work even if it is bad. Building one thing generates 10 more ideas. Then repeat product after product until something takes off.
  - Tech stack matters much less than starting; pick what's trendy. One or two hours a day gets you somewhere in a few months. No-code tools like Bubble also exist.

chunks.heading: Product and team management
chunks.text:
- Prioritization: he builds what makes his own life easier as a user. Backlog is only 2 to 3 weeks of work, because a long backlog is discouraging. He discards most feedback and only adds a request after hearing it two or three times.
- He doesn't heavily A/B test: he runs one or two tests at a time and doesn't optimize his landing page. One test on Revid showed that giving new users more free credits increased conversion, the opposite of his bet.
- Team: no meetings, no retros. He once promoted story points and sprints but now sees them as unnecessary. He works Founder Mode style, hands-on, with a small team of autonomous people. He says every question to him takes his time and the person's job is to take a topic fully off his plate.
- On PM roles: he believes product owner and product manager should be the same person, and that builders find the specs' mistakes by building, so detailed specs are less valuable.
- Time: 2 to 3 hours of deep work in the morning, then messaging, Twitter and other tasks. He tackles the big hard problems quickly instead of procrastinating.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo explains why he left venture-backed teams for lean bootstrapping: ship a product a week, follow revenue only, and kill what doesn't work. He covers equity-sharing with creators, an earn-out sale structure, the new modes in the AI era, and his equity-partnership model of buying or partnering on small products.

chunks.heading: Why Tibo left venture-backed startups and bootstrapped
chunks.text:
- His first two venture-backed companies "crashed." He says he is not a good manager and that school pushes you toward managing big teams.
- His lesson from those two: "You cannot create a good product with 10 interns."
- To reach product-market fit, he argues the founder must be hands-on, the most motivated person, and the one who can run the most experiments fastest.
- Having a big team felt good at the family dinner, but it didn't produce product-market fit.
- He chose bootstrapping partly for freedom. During covid he and his wife were nomading, and raising venture money needs investor meetings and a hired team.
- He recommends bootstrapping first. A founder who raises usually gives away a large share of equity, and AI has pushed the cost of building SaaS toward zero.
- He now gets offers from people wanting to invest and declines: "I honestly don't need money to create SaaS right now." Taking money "adds so many issues."
- If he did take money, it would come from other indie makers and founders who have done what he is doing and can give advice.

chunks.heading: Shipping one product a week and following only revenue
chunks.text:
- With his co-founder Tom (a micro founder duo, two people total), he tried to ship one product per week "until something sticks." It ran about four months, with roughly 10 to 11 products. The last one was Tweet Hunter.
- If an idea came out of a Zoom brainstorm, he would end the call and start coding it the same day.
- He says the process was "a nightmare at first" but it let them pivot quickly until they hit something valuable.
- His key rule: revenue was the only metric they followed. Free users and a few people saying they like it just reassure you, "your mom is going to tell you that your product is awesome." In his first two startups, free users kept them working on weak ideas.
- One product reached $300 in monthly revenue and they still killed it. They wanted to see $1K in monthly recurring revenue before going all in.
- He says $1K was not a magic number, just a strong signal.
- An even better signal than revenue: new users and signups still arriving on days when they weren't promoting anything, because they were heads-down building. That meant people found the product without being pushed.
- On killing projects: he says to "listen to the market," run experiments, double down on what works and "relentlessly" kill what doesn't.

chunks.heading: Sunk-cost mistakes and outsourcing development
chunks.text:
- His first startup took two years on an idea that should have taken three months to judge. After the initial four-month app didn't work, they raised money to build a better version of the same app, which he calls a mistake.
- This year he outsourced an app to a developer. It was meant to be a one-month project and was still not working after three months, with obvious poor fit between developer and idea.
- The trap: each "add two more weeks" increases the money spent, so you feel you can't kill it.
- He says outsourcing only works if you pay a very high package for top talent, or hire a junior and manage them closely. He did neither.
- His new approach is equity partnerships with people who have real skin in the game. He says "it's incredible how people are motivated when it's their ideas and not yours," so he mostly works on ideas that are not his.

chunks.heading: Equity partnerships on existing small products (Outrank, Feather)
chunks.text:
- Example: Outrank (outrank.so), a keyword and blog post generation tool that publishes a new blog post each day to rank on specific keywords.
  - He found a solo founder with about $300/month in revenue, which he sees as a real signal of value even if the packaging is poor.
  - They split equity. He got hands-on with the app, improved generation and prompting, and focused on distribution while the founder focused on building.
  - Launch: about 50 new free trials the day after launch, already at $2K monthly revenue, with a hope of $5K within weeks.
- How he finds targets: he scrolls Twitter/X, notices interesting products, engages and asks many questions. He says you must set up Twitter properly (lists, and tools like his own Super X) or you only see the day's viral memes.
- His staging, per product:
  - Month 1: build a working version of the shared vision and put it in users' hands. DM a few people for feedback.
  - Month 2: deliver more value and try to get a bit above $1K in revenue.
  - If that works, launch and then activate SEO and new acquisition channels.
- He puts in no money, only his time, his audience and his distribution channels. He thinks paying a founder cash while they hold some equity leaves them with less skin in the game.
- Feather: he wanted to buy it after selling Tweet Hunter. It had healthy metrics, very low churn and steady growth, and he was a user. During the acquisition, Feather raised prices so that he would pay 2.5x more ($100/month to $250/month).
  - He expected many users to be in the same spot, so he bought a second tool that sends newsletters from Notion, merged its capabilities into Feather and turned it into a newsletter tool. The newsletter feature was much harder to build than expected, but growth kicked in once released.
- On pricing: on Tweet Hunter he raised the price five times, always grandfathering existing users, with increases of about 20% or 30%.

chunks.heading: Micro-acquisitions: buy assets, not companies
chunks.text:
- He recommends buying assets or products rather than companies, because selling a whole company involves selling equity, paying tax and heavy contracts.
- He says when working at Tweet Hunter they acquired more than 10 tools, around $10K assets each.
- The process he describes: wire the seller $5K, receive all the assets, wire $5K more at the end. The contract is under one page, generated with GPT-4.
- He notes a company-level deal can still be needed for tax and accounting reasons.
- A similar speed point: another speaker's newsletter acquisitions took 30 minutes over Twitter DMs, and Tibo describes the same low-friction approach for small assets.

chunks.heading: Creator equity as a distribution engine (Tweet Hunter)
chunks.text:
- It started by accident at a little above $1K monthly revenue. He reached out to Twitter creators using the product, and one, GK Molina, asked to "get in" at co-founder level. His audience matched the target audience exactly.
- They gave him up to 25% of Tweet Hunter. It was "very generous."
- They then repeated it at a much smaller scale: 17 creators received 0.1% each.
- Result: about 17 big creators strongly incentivized to grow the product, so every feature launch and announcement had a pool of people pushing it.
- He stresses they didn't plan this; they listened to what creators hinted at and followed it.
- He mentions a related build: Mega-style creator partnership and sponsored post features are now being explored by others.

chunks.heading: Moats, building in public and platform risk in the AI era
chunks.text:
- Because AI makes copying easy, he says products are hard to defend. A newcomer can clone an app and sell it for half the price.
- The moats he sees:
  1. Proprietary in-house data.
  2. A distribution channel others lack (a YouTube audience is his example).
  3. Users and network effects (X, where even presidents and CEOs publish because most people listen there).
- Building in public: when he started more than three years ago it was clearly beneficial. Now he asks why share all your secrets when you have no moat. His view:
  - If you're a nobody with no audience, you have nothing to lose and it can be a great start.
  - With 100K followers, every thing you share gets copied, so you must be comfortable with 100 copycats fast.
  - The more engaged the audience, the more valuable it is, so it's a balance between that value and the copy risk.
- Platform risk is real. His LinkedIn account was suspended at one point, and his former LinkedIn product (Taplio) was 23% of revenue when he sold it in April, so he is relieved he sold it.
- He is building a new app for X again and worries about getting banned, since X is his primary platform. He also notes platforms are a black box, so no one knows whether falling engagement means algorithm changes, fewer bots or fewer users.
- On the future of SaaS: if AI can build full SaaS from a prompt, companies may build their own tools. Otherwise the market stays competitive but still values well-built software. He now often buys SaaS because he likes and wants to support the founder (example: Dan Chen of Testimonial), so personal brand becomes a buying reason.

chunks.heading: The Tweet Hunter and Taplio exit deal
chunks.text:
- The original plan: build to $10K monthly revenue, sell for $1 million in under a year, then start over. It didn't go that way.
- Tweet Hunter grew well past $10K monthly revenue, and no buyer would take it without the founders staying two years.
- The business was only about a year old, with risks: X under Elon Musk, and LinkedIn rule non-compliance.
- Deal structure: 20% of the price paid up front ($2 million) and 80% tied to performance milestones based on monthly revenue. There were six milestones that could take the total from $2 million up to $10 million. They unlocked five, for a final price of $8 million.
- He recommends creative earn-out structures in similar situations, but says the two years were very stressful. The milestones meant they worked even more than before, and there were Twitter and LinkedIn suspensions along the way. He believes they would probably have earned more by not selling.
- Today he would not accept any sale requiring a two-year stay, because he values his time far more.
- Buyer choice: big US and Indian companies made it hard to talk constructively. The buyer was a French company of about 60 people, with founders and executives easy to talk to.
- Negotiation tip: everyone focuses on the headline number, but the terms matter just as much, "the terms is going to make you bless your lawyer or want to kill him."

chunks.heading: Co-founders, multi-product strategy and personal beliefs
chunks.text:
- Goal: five companies at $100K MRR each within three years. He expects maybe two or three to hit that range, one around $10K to $20K and hopes one blows up well above $100K. He feels he is near maximum capacity at four products and says more than five would be crazy.
- He wants to build a strong acquisition engine across multiple products and cites Andrew Wilkinson's umbrella of companies as inspiration. He notes it goes against the usual "focus on one thing" advice. Each product has its own co-founder, so he won't be the only decision maker.
- Co-founders don't need managing, and with AI he says each of them is worth about 10 people from five years ago.
- Why Tom worked: easy to communicate frustration, they disagree often but want the same direction, and complementary styles. Tibo ships first and favors quantity over quality; Tom forces higher quality. They've known each other about 10 years.
- With new co-founders he is trying to take the "quality guy" role in some cases, and says it's not working yet.
- Co-founder issues: raise a latent problem early, because waiting only makes it harder and eventually you blow up.
- Product-market fit signal: "Founders never know when they need to quit but they definitely know when they need to continue." When he reached PMF, he was overwhelmed with support, growth and tech not holding up.
- First-time founders: take your first idea, ship it and show it, because it probably won't work but that is how you get feedback.
- His contrarian belief: quantity beats quality. He cites a study (he thinks Harvard) where a group graded on quantity produced the best papers.
- Burnout: after his first two ventures failed he went to court to close a company with debts and took a CTO job at a scale-up, which brought him into B2B SaaS. He advises not comparing yourself to others' posted revenue milestones, and keeping community, exercise, healthy eating and sleep.
- Newsletter and projects: tmaker.io.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo explains how he validates ideas by shipping many products fast, building tools he uses himself, and making each one 10x better at a single thing. He also covers single-price pricing, affiliates, user DMs for feedback, and why distribution compounds across a product portfolio.

chunks.heading: Building a lot of cheap products to find what sticks
chunks.text:
- Tibo says the most common first-time founder mistake is sinking years into one idea that isn't worth it. He did this twice, spending about two years on each, with basically no revenue, which he counts as roughly four years lost (though he learned skills that later made him a CTO and then an entrepreneur again).
- He blames wanting to "sell at all cost" and refusing to hear feedback that says the idea is bad. He also rejects the engineering-school advice to chase one billion-dollar "next Facebook" idea.
- His process on returning to startups was to ship one new product every week until something stuck. Over about four months he shipped more than 10 products. Some were tiny, some got a few hundred dollars in revenue, some got zero, and some were info-product landing pages (a lead model).
- Building more shows you what the market wants. You see quickly when a launch goes "to the void" and when a tweet about a product takes off, which you can't see by working on a single product.
- If you have no idea what to build, he says to pick the very first thing and start. It will probably fail, but it leads to hundreds of better ideas.

chunks.heading: Build products you use yourself, then look for others like you
chunks.text:
- His edge is building products where he is the user. He used each product daily, fixed friction and bugs right away, and collected feedback through Twitter DMs in a never-ending loop.
- Without this, you either spend huge effort understanding the end user's core need or end up with a surface-level view of the problem and fail.
- If a workflow is weirdly personal, he suggests recording everything you do and explaining why. The internet is large, so other people almost certainly share your habits.
- Big companies must go broad, so they skip niche workflows. His example is mind maps: loved by some, disliked by 80-90% of people, so big software ignores them. That leaves room for focused products that do just that very well.

chunks.heading: Ideas are not the edge: be 10x better at one thing
chunks.text:
- Tibo says there is nothing valuable in the idea itself. Tweet Hunter, Taplio, Revid and Outrank were all unoriginal ideas. His edge is being a "product person" who builds something at least 10 times better than competitors at one specific thing.
- "You have to do one thing extremely well", and then you can be average or good at everything else, as long as that one thing is very valuable to users.
- Taplio's one thing was actionable analytics. You could see the top-performing content of any LinkedIn account, find the best-performing formats, and repurpose a viral post into your own niche.
- Outrank's one thing: most SEO time goes into keyword research, not writing. It found high-volume, low-difficulty keyword opportunities, put them in a calendar, and each day generated a post for that keyword.
- What made Outrank take off was a backlink exchange. Because it had a large user base, it clustered users with similar content and created backlinks between their blog posts, raising domain authority. Users saw it as the cheapest and most efficient way to get backlinks, since AI means everyone can now generate a good post.

chunks.heading: How small the first version should be, and how to talk to users
chunks.text:
- The first Tweet Hunter was one feature: an input field where you typed a topic like "cold email" and got a wall of viral tweets on it. That alone got traction and justified building the rest.
- He notes that with AI everywhere, expectations are higher, so it is now hard to ship something that looks very rough.
- For a new product idea (a "backup" high-quality podcast recorder, discussed with the host), he warns that trust is the hurdle: losing a one-hour recording to a bug would be fatal, so early users need strong reliability signals. He advises being flexible and following what users actually care about rather than your original vision.
- On Tweet Hunter and other early products, the support button linked to his Twitter DMs. It opened a conversation (why did you do that, how would you push this further) instead of a bug email. "The forms are the worst. I would definitely not do that."
- His advice to newcomers: build real things and expose the work publicly, and have real conversations with people, which is the hardest part but where the knowledge about direction and opportunities comes from.

chunks.heading: Forking, pivoting and acquiring: the Revid story
chunks.text:
- Revid was originally Timeframe, a product video maker (script and music in, text animations synced to the beat). Tibo acquired it with a fixed $15k plus revenue share up to a total of $50k, which he paid off fully within 6 months. It was generating $3,000 per month at the time.
- The issue was that product videos are only needed once or twice, so he pivoted to social media and AI videos. At the time AI video was very glitchy, so value came from sourcing the best models and many hacks to fix generations.
- He did not kill Timeframe. He copy-pasted the codebase into a new repository, called it Revid, and ran both in parallel. When Revid took off he killed Timeframe, redirected its traffic, and merged them. Revid is his best product so far.
- He did the same earlier: Taplio was a fork of Tweet Hunter dedicated to LinkedIn. "Every product is an experiment", and he will kill, merge or fork as needed.

chunks.heading: Validating without an audience, and launching
chunks.text:
- He says the audience came from the successful products, not the other way around. When he started Tweet Hunter and Taplio he had about 900 followers on Twitter, which he says were 99% bots or dormant accounts.
- The audience formed from sharing the process: building a product a week, documenting wins and fails, and doing more SEO than other founders.
- You don't need thousands of followers to validate: DM a few relevant people and look for three or four replies on a tweet. Platforms are shifting from followers to reach and engagement, so good content can reach anyone.
- Product Hunt (he was Product Hunt maker of the year in 2022) is no longer a big traffic spike, but he still launches there for two reasons: a high-DR backlink (plus further backlinks from sites connected to Product Hunt) and an excuse to make noise to his audience.
- Founder Circle, his community, went from zero to $15K in about 36 hours with about 150 members. He says that was 100% his five years of audience and authority, and that managing a community is a lot of work and he's unsure he'll keep it alive because he prefers building products.

chunks.heading: Pricing: one offer, aimed at serious customers
chunks.text:
- Across his products the standard is a single price, often $99 per month (he mentions $49 to $99 as his range). Testing showed that more choices make it harder for users to convert, so he uses either one offer or a no-brainer option where the choice is obvious.
- Price is not set from cost: "the product and the cost is based on the price, not the other way around." He can deliver better or worse results by using better or worse AI models.
- Price selects your customer. Going from $9 to $49 to $99 brings in very different people: the higher the price, the more serious and successful they are, and they are more loyal if served well. People who want the best product don't mind paying a bit more for a 10% quality gain.

chunks.heading: Running several products and affiliates
chunks.text:
- He doesn't run multiple products alone: each has a different co-maker who can handle things when he focuses elsewhere.
- All his products target the same niche, small-team founders who want more sales and traffic. So one distribution action (his audience, newsletter, SEO, socials, ads) benefits every product.
- Affiliates: he uses an affiliate platform, tries to turn users into affiliates, and keeps them engaged weekly or monthly with content on what works and how top affiliates operate. One post mentioned affiliates making roughly $30,000 in a month (confirmed in the question, not stated by him).
- A tactic: find competitors' affiliates through tags in their links (such as "via" or "ref") using Ahrefs or Semrush.
- Affiliates accelerate growth but don't create it. People risk their reputation, so they only promote a high-quality product that already has proven growth and conversion.
- He remains bullish on software despite AI: developer job openings are rising again, one engineer now produces about 10x more, and he cites Stripe's reported 70% revenue growth. He expects a rotation in which software wins, not the end of the industry.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo explains why two VC-backed startups failed (no focus on revenue, big teams that couldn't pivot) and how he then shipped about 10 small projects in 4 months to find Tweet Hunter. He covers charging early, giving creators a small product stake for distribution, SEO mini-tools, and structuring the exit.

chunks.heading: Pivoting from VC-style startups to indie hacking
chunks.text:
- Tibo spent about 10 years launching startups and had several failures before Tweet Hunter and Taplio.
- His first two startups lasted about 2 years each. He raised money, hired big teams and chased user counts.
- He says he was not revenue-driven: "you're not revenue-driven". Users who didn't pay still reassured him, so he kept going.
- Raising funds and hiring a large team "completely stops you from pivoting quickly". Asking 3 of 15 employees to explore a new idea every week would burn them out.
- He argues the indie hacker or solopreneur advantage is waking up with an idea and testing it fast.
- A change of life (a child, travelling as a digital nomad, the start of COVID, no office) pushed him to work alone and without a team.
- He admits the solopreneur model is hard to make aspirational compared to Facebook or WeWork stories. Earning 6-7k per month does not make people dream.

chunks.heading: Launching a project every week to compress 2 years into 1 week
chunks.text:
- His goal was to compress the 2 years it took to learn a startup was failing into about 1 week.
- The target was a new project per week. In practice projects took up to 3 weeks, and some ran in parallel.
- He and Thomas launched about 10 projects in roughly 4 months, and the 11th was Tweet Hunter.
- Examples that didn't work:
  - A geolocated lead and email scraper for local businesses. It made about 2-3k€ from one big contract, then was dropped.
  - A tweet generator built on GPT-3, right after GPT-3 launched.
  - A Twitter analyzer using GPT-3. It reached about $300 MRR at $9/month (about 30 payers) but had high churn, so they dropped it.
  - A community search engine telling you where to promote a project. He says it fails because you can't drop a link in a community and expect sales.
- They asked for payment very early on every product, to avoid repeating the old mistake of measuring users instead of revenue.
- They reused the same payment system, accounts and backend on each project, which made each new launch fast. He compares this to Marc Lou's ShipFast boilerplate.

chunks.heading: How Tweet Hunter emerged
chunks.text:
- Twitter was becoming the main acquisition source of every project. Tibo and Thomas then wanted a bigger Twitter presence themselves and hit the problem of writing viral tweets.
- They built a search engine for viral tweets: the tool works out what you tweet about and shows high-reach tweets on similar topics. The first version was just a wall of tweets that refreshed.
- Tibo used it himself, and the wall sparked plenty of ideas for his own tweets.
- With only this feature, they reached $200, $300, $800 and even $1,000 MRR.
- He started with 1,500 followers, about 950 of them dormant. He says he was "nobody".
- The timing helped: 2021 was the creator-economy boom, so they shipped as people got interested in creating content on Twitter and LinkedIn.
- He frames building for a problem you have yourself as a solopreneur edge. The feedback loop is fast: use the product, see an issue, change a few lines, ship.
- Example: a user reported a bug in a DM, Tibo fixed it in about 5 minutes and replied that it was fixed. He says such users become your best advertising.

chunks.heading: Distribution: giving equity to creators and building in public
chunks.text:
- They sent Tweet Hunter to several big Twitter influencers. One loved it and joined the project, and the joint launch happened 3-4 months after the first version. In 2 weeks it took MRR from 3k to 18k.
- They then kept about 20% monthly growth for the following 6 months.
- That influencer got about 25% of the product's profit and 25% of the sale price of that product only. It was a distribution-style contract, not company equity, since the company held other projects.
- This worked well when they later built Taplio, a LinkedIn version of Tweet Hunter. Taplio now generates about twice what Tweet Hunter does.
- In January 2022, with Tweet Hunter at roughly 35-40k MRR, they onboarded 17 large Twitter creators and gave each 0.1% of Tweet Hunter.
  - The creators had "no concrete obligation". They were just asked for feedback, answers to questions and retweets of launches.
  - He says dropping the obligation unblocked everyone, and in practice they all did what was asked.
- He says this kind of move is easy when you're small, while a big company might take 18 months and many legal reviews.
- He says affiliate and referral programs are hard to launch before you are successful, because creators have hundreds of tools to promote and pick known ones.
