- They built in public and shared numbers and weekly updates showing a healthy, steady growth curve. He says this built trust and made creators want to join.

chunks.heading: Growth channels: SEO via mini tools and social
chunks.text:
- Tweet Hunter and Taplio have two main acquisition channels: SEO and social.
- The SEO channel is the mini-tool strategy. They extracted features as free, single-page, SEO-optimized tools.
  - Example: a LinkedIn stats checker, where searching a person's LinkedIn stats can land on their tool, which then pushes Taplio.
  - The LinkedIn video downloader gets about 1 million visits per month, as he recalls.
- They have about 15 mini tools on Taplio and about 15 on Tweet Hunter, built at a pace of roughly one every two weeks. Traffic accumulates as Google surfaces them.
- The social channel is people talking about them on LinkedIn and Twitter. Often there are no links, so many people search the brand name on Google, and he can't always tell where users came from.
- Context he gave: ARR reached 3 million in March and 5 million in June of a given year (recalled from his 2023 review); he said he didn't remember exactly what drove it.

chunks.heading: Team split and partnership
chunks.text:
- Tibo and Thomas split equity 50/50.
- Thomas is a pure product marketer. He handled acquisition (ads, SEO, landing pages), copy, brand text, product direction, design and wireframes.
- Tibo handled product, mockups and implementation, plus distribution, since he had the Twitter and LinkedIn audience.
- He says coding and writing positioning copy use totally different parts of the brain, so splitting the roles helps. As a dev, doing both is very hard, so he suggests compartmenting days (marketing one day, dev the next).
- Now that he launches projects without Thomas, he struggles on positioning and the deep pain point, and he calls Thomas "much better" at that. His larger audience makes distribution easier, though.
- His view: "it's hard to be on every front".

chunks.heading: Selling Tweet Hunter and Taplio
chunks.text:
- The initial plan with Thomas was to build a project to 10k MRR, sell it for $500k to $1M, and repeat. The product grew much faster and sold for much more.
- They hired a US broker and spoke with big US and Indian companies, including HubSpot. It was hard because:
  - they were small (around 15M ARR at the time);
  - churn was high and KPIs looked B2C even though the product was somewhat B2B;
  - they had only 12 months of track record.
- Acquirers also talked about being locked in for 2 years inside their culture.
- Tibo meanwhile had lunch with Guillaume Moubeche of Lemlist, who was already a Taplio customer. He had asked for 17 licenses so his whole team would post on LinkedIn.
- Lemlist had similar growth, a similar company size and a similar trajectory, so they chose it over a US buyer. They signed in summer 2022 and negotiated the terms and price in a WhatsApp group of three with Thomas.
- About 80% of the price was tied to growth milestones over the two years after the acquisition. That reduced risk for the buyer given high churn and acquisition dependence.
- Tibo insisted on keeping control of the products: "if you tie the whole value of the acquisition to milestones... you have to leave us the reins".
- Results: ARR was just over 15M at the sale and above 8M reported later in the conversation (he said they passed 8 million ARR, but the figure is ambiguous with the 15M mention, so treat with care). He expected to land just under the 100M ARR target; this figure is unclear as stated.
- Reasons to sell:
  - it was the plan from the start;
  - growth was so fast they needed help from people who had gone through similar growth, and Lemlist had;
  - they wanted to de-risk, having taken little cash relative to the company's value.
- Risks he named: platform dependency (Elon Musk's Twitter takeover) and Taplio not being fully compliant with LinkedIn's rules.

chunks.heading: Platform risk: the Twitter API price hike and LinkedIn
chunks.text:
- Twitter's API was free and then priced at $42,000 per month. After they asked to pay, access was cut off 3 days later (not 30), and support was gone after mass layoffs.
- About 48 hours later they found a contact, filled in the right form and started paying $42,000 per month, which they still do by manual transfer.
- Tibo says they could afford it, but he would never have built Tweet Hunter if he'd had to pay that from the start. He thinks it killed small players, and no new competitor has appeared in a year. He still finds the rule change "disgusting".
- On LinkedIn, the API is restrictive (no access to views or likes, no carousels, no mentions). They use a Chrome extension only for those gaps, with moderate usage, a nearby proxy per user and secure handling to protect user accounts. He contrasts this with heavier extensions like Waalaxy.
- He says they can adapt if LinkedIn changes things.

chunks.heading: Current projects and one-person company ambition
chunks.text:
- Tibo is working on Typefully-style video tools: TypeFrame (acquired) and Revid.ai, a spinoff.
- The idea is to apply the Tweet Hunter playbook to video: find viral videos, pull script pieces, repurpose content and let people without editing skills create videos for TikTok or YouTube Shorts.
- Revid reached more than $9,000 MRR. He has hired one full-time developer for the video editor, the hardest part.
- Tibo handles the search engine, transcription and AI generation parts, plus the landing page and blog.
- His longer-term ambition: a multi-product strategy with several products for the same audience (creators), promoted by sharing on Twitter and LinkedIn. He references Sam Altman's prediction of a one-person billion-dollar company, but says he is not that ambitious.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo explains why he bought out SuperX's co-founder, spent six months in stealth rebuilding it, and bet on X over LinkedIn after selling Tweet Hunter and Taplio. He argues growth on X needs good content plus a small circle of supportive friends, and that building for your own need produces a useful product.

chunks.heading: Why Tibo is all-in on SuperX and X growth
chunks.text:
- Tibo calls SuperX "the most important project I'm working on right now." He describes it as "what Tweet Hunter should be today if its new owners hadn't given up on it."
- He sold Tweet Hunter and Taplio in 2022 and left completely by 2024. He says the acquirer bought mainly for Taplio.
- He is "more of an X guy than a LinkedIn guy" and missed a tool that worked properly on X.
- His example of the acquirer's slow pace: when X launched long-form posts, Tweet Hunter took multiple months to ship support, while competitors had it in days.

chunks.heading: How Tibo came to own and rebuild SuperX
chunks.text:
- SuperX was first built by Hieu. Tibo joined him and they built a Twitter extension that was "quite successful."
- Tibo felt it was hard to grow with only an extension and that the product needed a web app.
- Hieu had different goals and lost motivation. Because the project mattered so much to him, Tibo bought Hieu's shares and looked for a new partner.
- He found Rob in February. The start was slow because some foundations were missing, so the product needed a complete revamp.
- They worked in stealth mode for 6 months. Tibo says the product only then became "actually useful," and he now uses it daily to schedule content, find inspiration and write better posts.

chunks.heading: What growth on X requires: content plus a support network
chunks.text:
- Tibo's framing of what you need to grow on X is two things: good content, and friends (a support network).
- He says SuperX is "not another schedule-your-content software." It aims to improve the content engine itself.
- The product is built around both sides: a Content Studio for content and a Social Hub for friends.

chunks.heading: The Content Studio: removing the blank-cursor problem
chunks.text:
- It combines strong inspiration features with a dedicated content studio that helps users write better.
- The goal is that nobody stares at a blank cursor wondering what to tweet.

chunks.heading: The Social Hub: a first circle of 10 supporters
chunks.text:
- Tibo says the Social Hub helps users build a strong first circle of friends who want to grow together, and that "that's how X actually works."
- His rule: you need a foundation of 10 incredibly supportive people who like and engage with everything you do.
- These people also support you during key moments of your X journey.

chunks.heading: Why Tibo is bullish on X as a platform
chunks.text:
- He is "incredibly bullish on X right now," citing Nikita Bier joining as a product guy. He believes X will dominate the social media space.
- His stated bet: "Many creators will get rich on X. I want to double down there."

chunks.heading: Building products you need yourself, and launch approach
chunks.text:
- Tibo says the product works and the foundations are solid, and he is seeing results from daily use. He frames this as "what happens when you build something you desperately need yourself."
- Before the public launch, he gathers feedback by asking readers about their biggest struggle growing on X.
- He builds an early-access list: readers reply "SUPERX" to be added.
- He runs a weekly newsletter (tmaker.io, 65k+ readers) and uses it as a distribution channel for his products, sign-off "Keep building."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo lays out a seven-step path from finding your edge to fixing retention. Ideas, not building, are the bottleneck now, so validate demand with a fake landing page, build in one week, find the real problem, scale acquisition fast, then obsess over retention.

chunks.heading: Know your edge before picking an idea
chunks.text:
Tibo defines business success in one phrase: "You have to be better than others at something." He starts by asking what makes the founder unique, then doubles down on it. His checklist:

- What skills do you have that others don't?
- Do you already have an audience?
- Any special market knowledge?
- A network you can leverage?
- A unique combination of skills?

He calls this your "unfair advantage" and treats it as the starting point of any new business.

chunks.heading: Build an idea bank because knowing what to build is the bottleneck
chunks.text:
Tibo argues that in 2025 "building is not a bottleneck any more. Knowing what to build is." He says 2025 is "ruled by idea guys", so founders should keep collecting more ideas, and he lists where to find them:

- Reddit questions ("goldmine of problems")
- Feature requests on Shopify, Webflow and similar platforms
- The Chrome extension store (ask what could be standalone)
- Amazon reviews, especially 3-star reviews of popular products
- App store complaints

His principle: watch what people complain about. "Their ignorance is your opportunity."

chunks.heading: Validate with a landing page and an email field before coding
chunks.text:
Tibo says to gauge demand before building, because there is no point building if no one is buying. His process:

1. Use V0 or Lovable to create a landing page.
2. Add one email input and a "Request Access" button.
3. Share it in DMs, tweets, Reddit and similar places.
4. See who gives you their email.

If people leave their email, that counts as validation. If there is no interest, skip to the next idea. His reasoning: if people won't commit to a product for free, you can't expect them to pay when you release it.

chunks.heading: Use the one-week build challenge to force a narrow core
chunks.text:
Tibo picks the landing page that collected the most emails and sets one constraint: "What can I build in ONE WEEK?" He insists on one week, not two, not a month, not a quarter. The limit forces the founder to narrow the product to its core value proposition.

- Build it, ship it, and get it in front of real people.
- He accepts that the first version will be "crappy", because the learning is worth it.

chunks.heading: Find the real problem behind the one you think you're solving
chunks.text:
Tibo says most founders miss that "the problem you think you're solving usually isn't the real one." He argues most problems come down to one of three things:

- Money
- Health
- Sex (relationships and status)

The founder should work out which one the product actually addresses, then go deeper, iterate, collect feedback and repeat.

chunks.heading: Expand acquisition fast once positioning is clear
chunks.text:
Once the founder has found the core reason to buy and the positioning, Tibo says to turbocharge client acquisition. Speed matters most, because "categories get saturated and sophisticated before you know", and you want to be the leader when that happens. His channel list:

- Build in public on X
- Start with basic Meta and Google ads
- Activate SEO, using Feather.so or Outrank.so to start quickly
- Create mini-tools for lead generation
- Work with influencers and set up an affiliate program (he names Rewardful)
- Build virality into the product by making it shareable

His rule: each channel properly built compounds.

chunks.heading: Fix retention because it beats acquisition
chunks.text:
Tibo warns that once there is traffic and some revenue, retention will likely be poor. He says this is where most founders fail: they keep acquiring users who just leave. His stance is "Retention > acquisition." He tells founders to work on it obsessively ("It's your oxygen"), because that is how a business compounds and how a founder reaches financial freedom.

He closes with the view that the difference between success and failure usually isn't the idea but "consistency. Persistence. Adjustment." He also notes that most people quit right before things get good, and that the playbook is simple but "simple ≠ easy."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo breaks a $1M SaaS down to roughly 350-700 paying customers, argues that copying the same idea-finding process as everyone else gives you the same ideas, and recommends building many products with strict 2-week validation windows. He gives four go/no-go questions and a fit test for choosing an idea.

chunks.heading: How Tibo reverse-engineers a $1M SaaS from the math
chunks.text:
- A $1M valuation at a 2.5x yearly multiple ("pretty normal for a saas") means $400k ARR, which is $35k MRR.
- $35k MRR is 350 customers at $100/month, or 700 customers at $50/month.
- "Your idea doesn't need to change the world. It just needs to find 350 to 700 people who will pay you consistently every month."
- Tibo says he has built a $1M SaaS five times: Tweet Hunter, Taplio, Revid.ai, Outrank.so and SuperX.so.
- Market-size check: "If you can't find 700 people who'd pay $50/month for your product, the market is too small. Start there before you write a single line of code."

chunks.heading: Why copying X trends gives you the same ideas as everyone else
chunks.text:
- "If you have the same process as everyone else, you'll have the same ideas as everyone else."
- Scrolling X, spotting a trending problem and building it puts you in competition with everyone who saw it at the same time.
- He describes two types of founders when it comes to finding ideas:
  - Founders with years in a specific industry, who know the pain better than anyone.
  - Founders with no deep industry knowledge and no obvious idea. Tibo was in this group in 2021.

chunks.heading: Industry insiders see what everyone else treats as normal
chunks.text:
- Existing companies often have deep incentives not to fix problems, because fixing them disrupts workflows or management structures.
- Examples he gives:
  - Elon saw that rocket parts cost a fraction of what NASA paid for finished rockets, and SpaceX was born.
  - The Loom founders were frustrated explaining bugs over email at their jobs. Screen recording existed, but nobody had made it seamless.
- "Your industry knowledge makes you see something obviously broken that everyone else has accepted as normal." He calls this the ideal scenario.

chunks.heading: The 10% rule: build many products instead of going all in
chunks.text:
- Tibo expects a success rate of 10% at best when creating new products, and says the same holds for Levelsio and Marc Lou.
- Going all in on one idea is "the worst thing you can do."
- A 10% success rate across 10 ideas means something works.
- He did "one product per week until something sticks" back in 2021, and says others have done it too.
- Why it works:
  - It forces you to ship instead of plan.
  - You get real feedback fast.
  - You move past the roughly 80% of ideas that will be garbage before they cost a year of your life.
- His summary: "Build more. Validate faster. Kill quicker."

chunks.heading: What makes an idea fit you specifically
chunks.text:
- An idea that could work won't necessarily work for you. It needs to fit:
  - Your skill set.
  - What you enjoy doing.
  - Something you can work on for a long time without getting bored.
  - The marketing style you're naturally good at, whether SEO, content, ads or 1-1 sales.
- Example: if you hate writing and hate SEO, a product that lives or dies on those channels will drain you fast. He mentions his tools Outrank (SEO on autopilot) and SuperX (content distribution) in this context.
- You can't know all of this from day zero. "The more you build, the more you understand what fits."

chunks.heading: The validation test: two weeks, four questions
chunks.text:
- Timeframe every idea, with a maximum of 2 weeks.
- At the end, ask four questions:
  1. Are people signing up without you chasing them?
  2. Are they coming back on their own?
  3. Are they paying without heavy convincing?
  4. Am I even getting feedback?
- Yes to all four: keep going.
- No to any: kill it and move to the next idea, unless there's an obvious fix.
- His conclusion: "A $1M SaaS idea isn't a flash of inspiration. It's what survives this process."
- Related rule: 2 hours of building for every 1 hour of content consumption.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo argues SaaS founders should work backwards from a price range ($29-$99) rather than use psychological pricing tricks. Low prices signal low quality, and raising Tweet Hunter from $9 to $49 cut conversion slightly but lowered churn and raised LTV. Price for the results delivered to people who badly need them.

chunks.heading: Price backwards from a range, not forwards from a trick
chunks.text:
- Tibo dismisses X pricing advice such as "Put $7 at the end of your price!", "Price it under $10!" and "Use psychological pricing!". In his words, "these tricks don't work."
- His rule: "You work backwards from the price point."
- He prices his SaaS in a range of $29-$99, then decides what to build, and how to build it, based on that range.
- Instead of obsessing over psychological pricing, he asks three questions:
  - What results do we deliver?
  - Who needs these results badly?
  - How much are these results worth to them?
- "That's your price."

chunks.heading: The low-price trap
chunks.text:
- Most founders start at $4-$9/month, believe it will attract more customers, and hope to raise prices "later". Tibo says "Later never comes."
- A low price is a low-quality signal. Customers perceive a cheap product as lower quality, so the price hurts the product.
- A low price does not compensate for low value. You can't price at $5 and expect users to tolerate a bad product.

chunks.heading: High-value clients don't care about price, if the problem is burning
chunks.text:
- Customers with a burning problem care about the result, not the monthly fee.
- Keyword research tools: if the data and opportunities are the best, it doesn't matter whether it costs $50, $100 or $200/month. The advantage outweighs the software cost.
- Newsletter software: deliverability matters more than saving $50/month. He says this is part of why many email companies scale to 7 figures quickly.
- The condition is that the product solves a burning problem. That is why his headline carries an asterisk: "High-Value Clients Don't Care About Price*".

chunks.heading: Tweet Hunter: raising prices 5x
chunks.text:
- Tweet Hunter started at $9/month and ended at $49/month, a 5x increase. The increases applied to new customers only.
- Each price increase had two effects at the same time:
  - A small drop in conversion.
  - Lower churn, which he says the team did not expect.
- Fewer people bought, but those who did stayed longer.
- "EVERY SINGLE TIME we raised prices, the LTV bump made for the conversion drop."

chunks.heading: Complaints about price are a good sign
chunks.text:
- People who complain about a price bump often love the product, because they rely on it.
- Most complainers don't actually churn.
- Real churn comes from customers who don't find the product valuable and cancel silently.
- His heuristic: "If no one's complaining about your price, it's too low."

chunks.heading: Solve a real problem first; higher prices create a upward spiral
chunks.text:
- The number one focus should be solving a real problem for the customer. That gives you the authority to charge more.
- Higher prices change how you operate:
  - You think bigger.
  - You build better features.
  - You deliver premium experiences.
  - Your users get better results.
- He calls it a win-win spiral upward.

chunks.heading: The pricing framework
chunks.text:
1. Price for results, not features.
2. Target people who value those results.
3. Don't fear raising prices.
4. Build for premium, charge for premium.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo's 2025 review of his multi-product portfolio, which grew 5.6x to $700k+ MRR. Product by product, he draws lessons on building tailwind businesses, turning customers into a growth loop, cutting losers, finding co-founders, and building a real audience over vanity followers.

chunks.heading: Portfolio results in 2025: from $125k to $700k+ MRR
chunks.text:
Tibo went from 5 projects at about $125k combined MRR to $700k+ MRR in 12 months (5.6x). He treats the portfolio model as the main lesson of 2025: revenue became "genuinely distributed" for the first time.

- While one product stagnated (Feather), four others grew. Revid was no longer about 95% of revenue.
- He says that financial security "changes how you think, build, and take risks."
- Product MRR, start to end of 2025:

| Product | Start | End |
|---|---|---|
| Revid.ai | $100k | $450k+ |
| Outrank.so | $12k | $250k |
| Feather.so | $10.8k | $10.3k |
| SuperX.so | $1k | $14k |
| PostSyncer.com | $0 | $2.6k |

- His summary lesson: "Build products that matter. Everything else follows."

chunks.heading: Build a "tailwind business" that gets better with every AI model release (Revid.ai)
chunks.text:
Revid grew the most in absolute dollars, from $100k to $450k+ MRR. Each new model (Veo 3, Sora 2, Gemini 3.0) first felt like an existential threat. The opposite happened: "Every new model made Revid better, not obsolete."

Why it worked, per Tibo:
- Revid is not just a wrapper around AI APIs. It built workflows users need without making them play with AI on their own.
- Short-form video needs speed and quality, and AI provides both.
- The team focused on high-quality output and niche content where bigger players don't compete.
- Deep integrations with TikTok, Instagram and YouTube create switching costs.

He calls Revid a "Tailwind business": it gets sharper when a better AI model runs in the background. He argues not every business becomes irrelevant with AI growth. His question for founders: "How can I build a business that grows alongside the fast growing tech?"

chunks.heading: Make customers part of the growth loop: Outrank's backlink exchange network
chunks.text:
Outrank grew from $12k to $250k MRR. Tibo says the team built something so valuable they didn't see it at first: the fastest, most effective way to get backlinks and grow Domain Authority. He says the harder problem is building authority that makes AI recommend you.

How the backlink exchange network works:
- Every user joins a pool automatically.
- Blogs reference relevant content from other users.
- Links add genuine value (not spam).
- Everyone's DR grows together, and network effects compound.

Tibo says this group growth model means customers win more and stay longer. He expects AI SEO to go mainstream, so more people will look for tools to grow their search presence. His question: "How can I make my customers an active part of my growth journey? Can this help them too?"

chunks.heading: Rescuing a stuck product with the right co-founder (SuperX)
chunks.text:
SuperX went from $1k to $14k MRR. It sat at $1k MRR for 10 months with his first co-founder, Hieu, and he almost killed it.

What changed after Rob joined:
- They rebuilt from scratch with a new architecture and a better user experience.
- Rob's product storytelling "made it click."
- The product was repositioned for how X actually works in 2025.

Tibo says "the right co-founder changes everything" and that Rob brought the missing piece he couldn't provide alone. He says SuperX is better than Tweet Hunter ever was, and Tweet Hunter hit $250k MRR at peak.

The challenge ahead is X's expensive API, where every post fetch costs more than an AI generation. His diagnostic question: "Are the skills I lack hurting my business? Is there anyone who can help me here?"

chunks.heading: Handing off a stagnating product (Feather)
chunks.text:
Feather was the only product that didn't grow ($10.8k to $10.3k MRR). Tibo says stagnation hurts more than failure because you keep hoping it'll turn around. He likes the product and says the tech is solid, but he couldn't crack growth.

- He made a deal with his business partner Pranav, who gets more shares and will run it fully on his own.
- He is looking for a GTM-focused person to join and scale it.
- His lesson: "You can't win in everything you do," and giving yourself that margin of error is okay. Sometimes the best move is handing a great product to someone who can focus on it.
- His prompt: "Am I working on a product that is not giving me the results I need? Is this time for a hard step?"

chunks.heading: Spotting ecosystem shifts (PostSyncer)
chunks.text:
PostSyncer went from $0 to $2.6k MRR, with a recent explosion. Tibo's reasons it's working:
- Platform fragmentation is real; Threads overtook X in users.
- Creators need presence everywhere but can't manage it manually.
- AI makes deep multi-platform customization possible.

He believes it already does more than giants like Buffer and Hootsuite for multi-platform AI posting. His question: "What recent changes in the business ecosystem can I take advantage of?"

chunks.heading: Audience as the foundation, and what he optimizes for
chunks.text:
Tibo says his business is largely built on his audience. Exposure to 170,000 followers helps validate ideas, find beta testers and get initial traction.

- **Social:** He stopped caring about follower count in 2025; only impressions and engagement matter. He focused on valuable content instead of growth hacks: "that's the real growth hack." He would rather have 1000 real builders than 10,000 random scrollers.
- **Newsletter:** His weekly email has 65,000+ subscribers, and 30,000+ read each week. He uses it to share behind-the-scenes of the business and invites replies.

chunks.heading: 2026 goals
chunks.text:
Tibo frames 2025 as proving the portfolio model works and 2026 as scaling what works and fixing what doesn't.

- SuperX to $100k+ MRR.
- PostSyncer past $50k MRR.
- Figure out Feather's future, with or without him.
- Keep Revid and Outrank growing sustainably.
- Launch at least 1 new product.
- Invest in 5+ indie products.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo argues bootstrapped founders should skip "blue ocean" invention and instead rebuild an existing product for the user the market leader ignores. He gives a three-question framework for picking where to compete and cites Mark Pincus's repeat-copy playbook.

chunks.heading: Why Tibo copies existing products instead of inventing new ones
chunks.text:
- Tibo runs a portfolio at $1M MRR across 5 products. None are original ideas. Short video (Revid.ai), SEO automation (Outrank.so) and scheduling tools (PostSyncer.com) all existed before his versions.
- He did not find untouched markets. He found crowded markets where one type of user was being ignored and built something better for them.
- His rule: the category already exists, and the job is to own a corner of it better than anyone else.
- Notion (note-taking), Figma (design software) and Slack (team communication) were not first in their categories, yet each became the go-to product.

chunks.heading: Why he rejects Blue Ocean thinking
chunks.text:
- He argues the 2005 book "The Blue Ocean Strategy" (find empty markets, invent new categories, be the next Facebook) sold over 4 million copies and produced almost no successful bootstrapped founders.
- It is good advice for building a $10B company, but bad advice for building a business in general. "You don't want to risk your entire life at a 1% chance of success."
- The model only really worked for VCs. They need moonshots because one win has to cover 99 losses in their fund.
- For a founder with a limited number of attempts, one loss can be dramatic.
- He fell for it coming out of university: years spent trying to invent something nobody had built, "years wasted, almost no money earned."
- His closing question: are you building for a 1% shot at $1B or a 50% shot at $1M? That answer defines how you think, build and learn.

chunks.heading: The question to ask about every product: Mark Pincus's approach
chunks.text:
- Tibo cites Mark Pincus, who launched 10 products, 8 of which became hits, without ever inventing a new category. FarmVille was a farm simulation game and Words With Friends was a word game like many others.
- Pincus asked one question each time: "What does the best possible version of this look like for the person being ignored by the current market leader?"
- Tibo says that question is worth more than any original idea.
- He notes Pincus calls the resistance to copying "moral arbitrage". School taught us copying is cheating, and that guilt keeps the edge available for whoever drops the ego first.

chunks.heading: Three-question framework before building anything
chunks.text:
1. **Who is already paying for a solution to this problem?** If nobody is paying, the problem is not painful enough. "Full stop."
2. **Who is that solution not working for?** Every market leader ignores someone: they get too big, too bloated, or too focused on a certain kind of client. That gap is where you live.
3. **What would make that person switch today?** Not eventually, immediately. That is the one thing to be meaningfully better at.

chunks.heading: Why incumbents leave the gap open
chunks.text:
- Existing companies will not fix the gap themselves. Solving it disrupts their workflows, upsets current customers and threatens their pricing model.
- They have every incentive to leave the problem open, and you have every incentive to close it.
- This makes a neglected segment of a proven market a more reliable opening than a new category.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo explains why he, having raised VC before, now bootstraps: investor money creates fake validation, VC power-law math pushes you toward lottery-ticket growth instead of a free profitable business, and most internet companies only need paying users. He reports $1M MRR across 5 bootstrapped, profitable products.

chunks.heading: Why Tibo says VC money is not validation
chunks.text:
- Tibo has raised VC before, and says that is exactly why he won't again. His reasons: what it does to "your math, your mindset, and your freedom before anything even goes wrong."
- When a VC writes a check, a founder feels validated, as if smart people with pattern recognition said yes and so the idea must be right.
- That feeling cost him two years, twice. He kept building products nobody was buying because he "confused investor confidence with market demand."
- His rule: "VC money is not user validation. It never was." The only validation that counts is someone opening their wallet and paying for the product. "Everything else is noise."
- On congratulating founders for raising: it is like congratulating a chef on getting the vegetables. The meal hasn't been cooked yet.
- His closing line to readers: "user validation over investor validation. Always."

chunks.heading: How VC math works against founders
chunks.text:
- VCs run a power law model. They expect 9 out of 10 bets to fail and need just one company per fund to return everything.
- So they are not optimising for a founder's sustainable, profitable, free life. They are optimising for a lottery ticket that pays 100x.
- If a business is doing well but not on a billion-dollar trajectory, investors stop caring. They give no more money and respond coldly.
- The pressure then starts:
  - The founder chases growth numbers someone wrote on a whiteboard.
  - They stop building for users and work just to raise the next round.
  - Tibo says they lose "80% of the freedom you started building for."

chunks.heading: Why Tibo stays bootstrapped (and may never sell)
chunks.text:
- When you bootstrap and your products print cash, there is no pressure to exit and nobody writing numbers on paper for you to follow.
- Because of this, he says he'll probably never sell again either.
- Status as of June 2026: $1M MRR across 5 products, every one bootstrapped and profitable.
- He says the best part isn't the number. It is feeling completely free to move fast, change direction, double down, or slow down, whatever feels right for the business.
- He says that freedom is why he started building in the first place.
- His background: built Tweet Hunter and Taplio (sold for $8M). He is now growing revid.ai, feather.so, superx.so, outrank.so and postsyncer.com.

chunks.heading: The rare cases where VC makes sense
chunks.text:
- Tibo isn't anti-VC entirely. He sees two cases where it genuinely fits:
  - True infrastructure plays where you need scale before revenue.
  - Regulated industries where compliance costs are very high.
- His view: most internet businesses don't need it. "You need users who pay. That's the only math that matters."

chunks.heading: The question to ask before raising
chunks.text:
- His test: "Are you raising because you need the money to build, or because raising feels like progress?"
- If it's the second, his advice is to go find a paying customer instead. "That's real validation."
- He also points to the horror stories common among founders who raised, such as:
  - A GP falling asleep during a $15M pitch.
  - Term sheets signed but the money never wired.
  - A founder offering his co-founders' stock in exchange for firing them.
- He says almost every founder he knows who raised has a story like this, but the deeper problem is the false validation and the loss of freedom.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo explains how he and co-founder Eugene took Outrank from a $300 MRR AI blog generator to $300k MRR in 15 months. The keys were repositioning as SEO infrastructure, building a backlink exchange network as a moat, and flipping the "AI killed SEO" fear into a growth narrative.

chunks.heading: Repositioning a stuck product: Outrank from $300 MRR to $300k MRR
chunks.text:
- Outrank (co-founded with Eugene) was a $300 MRR AI blog generator about 15 months before April 2026. Eugene had grinded on it alone with nothing moving the needle.
- Tibo joined in January 2025 and saw an "autonomous SEO machine" rather than a content tool. His takeaway: "Positioning beats features every time."
- The product was framed as "AI blog writer" in a sea of AI blog writers. It was repositioned as "SEO automation platform that builds your web presence while you sleep."
- "Different frame → Different outcome." The product barely changed; the framing did.
- Result by April 2026: $300k MRR, 2,500+ websites, 50,000+ articles generated per month.

chunks.heading: Finding a moat when content is a commodity
chunks.text:
- Tibo argues a moat is a defense against uncertainty and competition, which matters especially in the age of AI.
- "Content alone has no moat." GPT, Claude and Gemini all produce readable articles, so writing quality alone gives nobody a reason to choose Outrank.
- The moat he built is a backlink exchange: every Outrank user joins a backlink network. When Outrank generates an article, the AI links to relevant posts from other users' sites.
- Links are contextual, not random. Example: an email marketing article links to another user's email subject line guide, and a SaaS metrics article links to your churn article. These are real backlinks from real sites in adjacent niches.
- On the Google penalty worry: most agencies insert links with zero relevance and Google detects that. Outrank only adds contextually matched links that add value for the reader, which Tibo says Google rewards.
- Reported results: 25,000+ backlinks added, 750,000+ articles created. One user after 49 days: "DR jumped from 5 to 25. All I did was set up the blog."
- Lesson: "Network effects turn commodities into moats." A backlink network that gets more valuable with every user can't be copied overnight.

chunks.heading: Why the network advantage compounds
chunks.text:
- Tibo says network effects don't grow in a straight line. With 2,500 websites in the pool, each user can be matched with 2,500 potential linking opportunities.
- At 10,000 websites he expects value not just to quadruple but to "explode."
- Reasons he gives:
  1. More topical coverage gives better contextual fits.
  2. More niche diversity gives higher relevance scores.
  3. More volume gives more linking opportunities per article.
  4. The whole network's domain authority rises together.
- "We're not in the AI writing business. We're in the 'make sure AI can find you' business."

chunks.heading: Owning the narrative: "AI didn't kill SEO"
chunks.text:
- During a period when viral X threads daily claimed "ChatGPT killed SEO," Tibo took the opposite view and built the messaging around it.
- His reasoning: ChatGPT doesn't magically know about your tool. It searches Google and Bing to decide what to recommend, so to be recommended by AI you need to own the web.
- Practical implication: more articles, more backlinks and more presence in search results. Pages with better rankings appear more often in AI responses, and one well-optimized article can show up in thousands of AI conversations.
- He says OpenAI's Atlas launch in early 2026 validated this: web presence is how you get into LLMs.
- Lesson: "Position into the fear, not away from it." Everyone said AI is killing SEO; Outrank said AI makes SEO more important than ever. "The narrative that wins gets the customers."
- The narrative also gave customers a reason to accelerate rather than pause.

chunks.heading: Outrank growth timeline and which levers worked when
chunks.text:
- January 2025: $300 MRR, Eugene's original product; Tibo joins.
- March 2025: $10k MRR after a Product Hunt launch and repositioning as SEO infrastructure.
- May 2025: $40k MRR once the affiliate program kicked in. One affiliate made $3k in a single month.
- Late 2025: $200k MRR.
- April 2026: $300k MRR.
- Three levers by stage:
  - Early: distribution. Tibo had the audience and insights, Eugene had the product, and they launched.
  - Middle: product results. Users seeing measurable growth, plus testimonials.
  - Late: narrative. The AI-resilience argument.
- Lesson: "What works at $10k MRR doesn't work at $200k MRR."

chunks.heading: Pricing and product focus for Outrank
chunks.text:
- Pricing is deliberately simple: $99/month for 30 articles. "No credits. No tiers. No confusion."
- That works out to $3.30 per article, and Tibo says the math works in their favor given everything included in the product.
- Tibo says he generally doesn't do discounts because they devalue what's been built. He made an exception with a 20% off first month code ('TIBO') for his newsletter readers.
- Next focus areas:
  - Content quality for ranking and for AI citation: deeper brand voice matching, richer article structures, more content formats. A monthly update aimed at articles that "sound like an expert wrote them, not a content mill."
  - Compounding the backlink network.

chunks.heading: The meta-lesson for builders
chunks.text:
- Tibo credits Outrank's success not to AI writing ("Anyone can build that") but to two things:
  1. Network effects through contextual, relevant backlink exchange.
  2. Narrative positioning that turned AI fear into acceleration.
- His summary: "Find the moat. Own the narrative. Move fast."
- He ends by asking builders what they are building that might just need different positioning, implying a stuck product often needs reframing before more features.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo argues retention is a high-margin system that compounds, unlike acquisition, which resets every month. He gives five levers: filter feature requests instead of complying, build systems, raise prices to change who your customer is, make customization a moat, and tie customers' own success to your product.

chunks.heading: Retention is a system you build once; acquisition is a sprint you repeat forever
chunks.text:
- Tibo calls acquisition "a sprint you repeat forever": find someone, convince them, close them, repeat next month. It is expensive and the lowest-margin part of the business.
- Retention is "a system you build once". It is high margin, compounds instead of resetting every month, and is what stacks MRR and builds enterprise value.
- Founders over-invest in acquisition because it is visible and urgent. Retention gets ignored because it is quiet.
- He admits retention isn't glamorous (no screenshots to post on X), but says "this will make you rich."
- He lists five retention levers: filter requests, build systems, raise pricing, make customization a moat, tie customer success to the product.

chunks.heading: Stop complying with every request: filter feedback instead
chunks.text:
- Tibo says building exactly what every complaining user asks for is the mistake "almost everyone makes", and AI making building easier is making it worse.
- Adding every request makes the app do too many things, and new users get confused about the core function.
- His rule: the founder's job "isn't to comply. It's to filter." Get the feedback, then check whether the request aligns with what you're building.
- Two tests before saying yes:
  1. Protect margin: some value should stay reserved for higher tiers.
  2. Protect differentiation: if the workflow was built to differ from what already exists and the request erases that difference, don't build it.

chunks.heading: Revid.ai example: saying no to manual control is the product
chunks.text:
- Most AI video tools give users micro control. Revid.ai bet differently: AI models keep improving, and people want to save time, not micromanage a timeline.
- Instead of manual scene-by-scene editing, Revid tries to generate a full 2-minute video out of the box that does what the user actually wanted.
- Revid gets many requests for more manual control. Tibo says saying yes to all of them would make it "exactly like every other AI video tool out there."
- His conclusion: "Saying no to that request is the reason people choose Revid."

chunks.heading: Build systems, not patches
chunks.text:
- When solving a user's problem, ask whether you patched one instance or built something that prevents the whole category of problems.
- "Systems compound. And your revenue compounds with it."

chunks.heading: Raise prices to reduce churn (Tweet Hunter: $9 to $49/month)
chunks.text:
- Tweet Hunter started at $9/month, was raised over time, and ended at $49/month.
- The expected outcome was more churn. The actual outcome was the opposite: "Higher prices meant lower churn."
- At $9/month, people sign up on a whim and cancel the moment something feels slightly off, because there is no real commitment.
- At $49/month, people are already convinced it needs to work for them, have skin in the game, and try to make it work.
- Takeaway: "Higher pricing doesn't just increase revenue per customer. It changes who your customer is."

chunks.heading: Customization as a moat
chunks.text:
- The more a user configures a product around their exact workflow, the harder it is to leave.
- Tibo treats customization as more than a feature: it is a retention mechanism.

chunks.heading: Tie customer success to the product (Outrank.so example)
chunks.text:
- When a user's own success is built on top of what you made, they are far more likely to stay.
- Example: every great SEO case study for Outrank.so used it extensively, with 30 articles a month, backlink matching with a partner website, and a DR increase.
- If those customers wanted to churn, they would have to do all of that, and more, themselves. They are already getting results, so they stay.
- Tibo ends by asking readers how many months their average customer stays, as a way to make retention a number founders track.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo explains why his small-team SaaS products require a credit card before a free trial, why a free tier must earn its keep as acquisition cost, and why bootstrapped B2B founders should charge $40-$100/month instead of $9. He also argues for constant one-metric-at-a-time A/B testing and for choosing a model that fits your own constraints.

chunks.heading: Why Tibo requires a credit card before the free trial
chunks.text:
- Tibo's products usually ask for a credit card before anyone can try the free tier. Users enter a card, start a trial, and can cancel anytime.
- He knows people tell him he is "leaving money on the table", since the industry standard is to let people try without a card. His answer: "They're probably right - but I don't care."
- Without a card gate, users sign up, click around for a few minutes and leave. Before leaving, they send support emails about things already answered in the docs. At 500 free signups a week, support gets swamped by people who were never going to pay.
- Most of his products are run by two people (him and a co-maker). A few have three to four, and none have more. A small team cannot absorb that flood.
- A card creates commitment. People who enter one are serious, so they set the product up and give it a real shot. He says this brings higher-quality feedback, higher-quality users and a higher trial-to-paid conversion rate.
- The trade-off is lower volume, which he accepts: "I'd rather have 100 serious trials than 1,000 people who sign up and ghost."
- Card-gating works for B2B products that need setup time, complex tools that need configuration, and small teams that can't scale support.
- It does not work for viral consumer apps where volume is the game, simple tools with nothing to configure, or large teams with dedicated support infrastructure. He says to know which one you are before changing your model.

chunks.heading: Free tier: customer acquisition cost or charity
chunks.text:
- Tibo reframes the question from "should we have a free tier?" to "what job is the free tier doing?"
- If the free tier builds word-of-mouth and filters for people who will upgrade later, it is a customer acquisition cost. You pay in server costs, support time and feature work to find buyers.
- If it only serves people who will never pay, it is charity.
- AI products make this sharper. In 2019 a generous SaaS free tier cost almost nothing. In 2026 every free interaction with an AI product costs real money through API calls.
- He says this is why many AI tools deliberately limit their free tiers: they avoid subsidizing infinite usage from people who will never pay.
- His test: does the free tier bring people who eventually pay, or just people looking for free stuff? If you can't answer with actual data, "you don't have a freemium strategy. You have a free product with some paying customers on the side."

chunks.heading: A/B testing as a pricing and conversion habit
chunks.text:
- Tibo says he runs hundreds of experiments, "because guessing what to do in business is really expensive". He notes everyone has heard of A/B testing and almost nobody does it.
- Mechanism: each new signup is assigned a variable. If it is 1 they see landing page A, if 2 they see landing page B, and so on. Then you track the success metric and see which variant wins.
- Example from Revid.ai: the export button is shown in several ways (bigger, different copy, higher on the page). The metric is exports per session, and the variant with the most exports wins.
- Things to test:
  - Landing page headlines
  - Pricing display, such as monthly vs annual first
  - Feature prominence in the dashboard
  - Onboarding flows (number of steps, order)
  - CTA copy ("Start free trial" vs "Try it now" vs "Get started")
- You don't need a big system. He uses PostHog and Amplitude, and focuses on one metric at a time.
- His loop: "Pick the metric. Test the thing. Ship the winner. Move to the next test."
- His closing principle: keep testing new things, because that is what leads to compounded growth.

chunks.heading: Charge more: $99/month beats $9/month for small B2B teams
chunks.text:
- Tibo's "semi-controversial" take is that more indie hackers and small teams should make their apps fully paid and charge more, not less.
- Typical failure: a founder launches at $9/month because they fear nobody will pay $49. They get 200 users at $9, spend all their time on support, and can't afford help.
- The alternative: launching at $99/month, getting 20 users, making similar revenue, and having time to improve the product.
- Charging more forces a better product. At $99/month customers expect it to work, which pushes you to ship features that matter, fix bugs immediately and care about performance. In his words: "$9/month lets you get lazy. $99/month doesn't let you hide."
- Freemium creates a massive support load because every free user has questions and expects features. A team of 1-3 people can't handle that.
- His advice: make it paid, and expensive enough that only people who need it will pay.
- For business software, he says the $40 to $100 per month range works well. Buyers at that price expect ROI, and they stay if the product delivers and leave if not, which he calls "a clean signal".
- This does not apply to consumer apps or tools for teenagers, which are a different game of lower prices and higher volume.
- His conclusion for B2B SaaS: "$99/month beats $9/month every time."

chunks.heading: Price for your own constraints, not other companies' constraints
chunks.text:
- Tibo warns against copying what works for other companies, because they have different constraints.
- His rule: "Build for the constraints you have, not the ones you wish you had."
- Team size, support capacity, product complexity and marginal cost per user (especially for AI products) should decide whether you use a credit-card gate, a free tier, or a high-priced paid-only model.
- The one non-negotiable across all pricing models is continuing to run experiments.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo walks through seven products he shut down (ProductLift, Tweet Butler, ConvertRec, GeoLeads, AnimStats, Daily Nuggets and others) and the lesson each taught. The recurring themes are daily/weekly use, timing, avoiding custom work, choosing the right customer type, and unit economics. He argues fast, cheap failures are the best education.

chunks.heading: Why Tibo kills products: recurring use beats one-time value
chunks.text:
- Tibo says people only see his wins (Revid.ai at $600k MRR, Outrank.so at $300k MRR, SuperX.so at $25k MRR), never the 7 products he killed. He frames each as a datapoint: "Every 'failed' product made my next product better."
- ProductLift was a search engine for communities where people post when they launch. It got a few sales, then nothing. People only launch once, maybe twice if they pivot.
- His rule: "You can't build a recurring business on something people need once." If the problem comes up once, "you don't have a SaaS."
- He now builds only tools used daily or weekly. Examples: Outrank's backlink checker (used every week), Revid's video editor (used for every piece of content), SuperX's AI features (used daily).
- "Recurring revenue = recurring value."

chunks.heading: Monthly subscriptions need high-frequency use cases (AnimStats)
chunks.text:
- AnimStats made short animations from stats. It reached $1k MRR quickly, then stagnated because churn was brutal.
- People make stat animations about once per quarter, "maybe". Users subscribed, created 3 animations, cancelled, and came back months later.
- It was the opposite problem from ProductLift (used once ever); once per quarter still doesn't justify a monthly subscription.
- "High churn kills growth. You're running on a treadmill, replacing churned users instead of growing."
- Takeaway: only build products with daily or weekly use cases.

chunks.heading: Timing: some ideas are just too early (Tweet Butler)
chunks.text:
- Tweet Butler generated tweets with GPT-3 in 2021. The outputs were robotic and generic, and nobody wanted to post them. He killed it in 2021.
- By 2022, GPT-4 was good enough that the AI feature in Tweet Hunter became one of the most used parts of the product. He later sold Tweet Hunter for $8m.
- "Timing is everything." Some ideas are "2 years too early. That doesn't make them bad ideas. It makes them bad ideas for right now."
- He credits SuperX working partly because he learned to wait for the technology to be ready.
- His test for a struggling project: is it a bad idea or bad timing? Sometimes the answer is "kill it", sometimes "wait 6 months and try again". "Knowing the difference is the entire game."

chunks.heading: A feature is not a product, and custom work is not a product
chunks.text:
- Tweet Butler Digest delivered AI-powered Twitter analytics by daily email. It hit $300 MRR quickly, then stalled. People wanted a full dashboard to dive into, not analytics in their inbox.
- He notes $300 MRR felt like validation but wasn't: people tried it because it was cheap. "A feature pretending to be a product will always feel incomplete." Products must be complete solutions.
- ConvertRec made GIFs and short videos for product launches. He "accidentally made an agency": every client needed custom work, and AI wasn't good enough to automate it.
- He dislikes running agencies: you trade time for money, can't scale without hiring, and every client needs hand holding.
- "If you have to do custom work for each customer, you don't have a product." And: "If a product can't work without me, it's not a product, it's a service."

chunks.heading: Customer type matters more than revenue (GeoLeads)
chunks.text:
- GeoLeads scraped geo-based leads from Google Maps. It reached $1k MRR, but the best customers were enterprise clients who needed daily communication and lots of calls, which he hates.
- "$1k MRR from the wrong customers is worse than $0 MRR." He killed the product because it attracted customers he didn't want to serve.
- This changed his positioning: "My products are self-service or nothing."
- He credits Outrank.so working partly because he learned to avoid enterprise clients.

chunks.heading: Unit economics from day one (Daily Nuggets)
chunks.text:
- Daily Nuggets was personalized daily news tailored to your interests. Traction was low and costs too high: AI, data and delivery costs make personalized news expensive infrastructure.
- He also realized people want the take of someone they see as an expert. That is authority, and "AI doesn't have authority."
- OpenAI later built essentially this exact product into ChatGPT. His lesson: "being right about an idea doesn't matter if you can't make the economics work." Sometimes you're right but too small to execute.
- "Unit economics matter from day one."

chunks.heading: Launch fast, kill fast: cheap education
chunks.text:
- He killed these products in weeks or months, not years. Each cost him less than $5k and a few weeks of time. He contrasts this with founders who spend 2 years building something nobody wants.
- His summary: "Launch fast. Kill fast. Learn fast." "Fast failures are cheap education."
- Revid.ai works because he learned recurring use matters; Outrank.so because he learned to avoid enterprise clients; SuperX.so because he learned to wait for the technology.

chunks.heading: Why he still writes a weekly newsletter
chunks.text:
- Responding to a claim that nobody making $1M/month would write newsletters, he says he still shows up weekly because of the trust it builds and the support from readers.
- He cites DMs from readers: one closed a first SaaS client using his DM templates, one killed a bad idea after reading about validation (saving 6 months), and three started building their first product after seeing it's possible.
- He asks readers to reply with one thing they got from the newsletter, reads every reply, and often writes back. He calls this "not something you can automate".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo explains his model of how Twitter and LinkedIn distribute content: followers matter little, and posts spread circle by circle based on engagement. He draws action points: make engaging content, use short video, and engage with people around you.

chunks.heading: Why Tibo says social growth works differently in 2024
chunks.text:
- Tibo's core claim: "every platform is becoming TikTok. And your followers don't matter."
- An account with 150 followers can go viral, and an account with 100k followers can stay "pretty much dead". He says he has many examples.
- He contrasts this with the old days, when a post like "Best websites you don't know about" could pull 30k+ likes.
- His view in August 2024 is that growth on Twitter and LinkedIn is slow, with low impressions and less engagement.
- Because followers matter less, content quality decides reach. In his words, "No one is at a disadvantage when it comes to content."
- Smaller accounts get a real chance to reach more people.

chunks.heading: How the circle model of distribution works
chunks.text:
Tibo describes the algorithm as circle-by-circle distribution. He says he dug into it and shared his learnings on Twitter too.

1. **People are sorted into circles.** The platform groups every profile that has viewed or interacted with your content. Circle A holds the people most likely to engage, then circle B (engage less), then C, D and so on.
2. **Your content and profile are graded.** The better your content performs, the higher your grade. A higher grade means bigger circles.
3. **Content is distributed circle by circle.**
   - A post is shown to circle A first.
   - If circle A interacts, it goes to circle B, then C, and so on.
   - When engagement falls below a threshold, Twitter and LinkedIn stop showing the post to new people.

chunks.heading: Engagement beats audience size: create content that hooks
chunks.text:
- Tibo says "Engagement is queen." Big accounts used to be read "because you were you", even when the content was boring.
- Now, if content is not engaging enough, it never reaches your own audience.
- His recommended strategy is to create content that keeps people hooked.
- That may mean content that is more surface level and covers a wider audience.
- You then funnel those people into your newsletter for a deeper conversation.
- He sees "No more posting into the void" as a consequence of this model: good, engaging content gets the eyeballs it deserves.

chunks.heading: Short-form video as a distribution lever
chunks.text:
- Tibo argues video will always perform better because it retains users better. All platforms will use it to increase average time spent on the platform.
- He calls it the best time to start making short-form videos.
- One short-form video can be reused across five placements:
  - 1 Instagram reel
  - 1 YouTube short
  - 1 LinkedIn video
  - 1 Twitter video
  - 1 TikTok

chunks.heading: Be social to build your circle A
chunks.text:
- Tibo: "The best way to grow on social media… is by being social."
- He says you can't win in isolation anymore.
- Engaging with people around you boosts your own metrics.
- It also brings new friends, business partners and clients.
- Those people become your "Circle A". If they love your content, they engage with it, which makes it easier to reach circle B and so gives more reach.

chunks.heading: Tools Tibo is building around this model
chunks.text:
- He says content matters more than ever under this algorithm, which is why he is building SuperX (superx.so), which he calls one of the best tools to find gem content.
- A feature he is excited about studies the accounts that interact with you and gives the most accurate guess of your circle.
- His team also made a free tool to check your Twitter archetype at superx.so/creators.
- His background in the byline: he built Tweet Hunter and Taplio (sold for $8m), and is growing revid.ai, feather.so, superx.so, outrank.so and postsyncer.com.
- He shares weekly growth tips through his newsletter at tmaker.io, which he says has 65k+ readers.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo, who built Tweet Hunter and Taplio (sold $8m), lists 15 blunt lessons about building a business. The throughline is action over information: talk to users, cut features, ship many products, launch embarrassing V1s, charge more, and ignore ego, courses and fear of competition.

chunks.heading: Talk to users before you build
chunks.text:
- Tibo says "You're not talking to enough users. I know you think you are, but you're not."
- Every successful product he built started with dozens of conversations. Every failure started with assumptions.
- His instruction: "Stop coding. Start calling."

chunks.heading: Subtract features instead of adding them
chunks.text:
- He argues a product needs "fewer, better" features, not more.
- He has never seen a product fail because it did too few things well. He has seen hundreds fail because they did too many things poorly. His rule is to cut ruthlessly.
- He warns against ego-driven features. A fancy feature is often wanted because it is interesting to build, not because it earns revenue.
- He admits he used to focus on things that would make him look cool "at family dinner".
- His rule: focus on revenue, kill fast, because "ego costs money."

chunks.heading: Volume of shipped products creates luck
chunks.text:
- Tibo says success comes from creating more, which means shipping more, not coding more.
- He launched 10+ products before finding winners. Most people launch one or two and quit.
- His formula: "Volume creates luck. Luck creates success."
- Finishing matters. Unfinished projects in folders count for nothing until they are live.
- A finished mediocre product beats a perfect unshipped one every time. His rule is to ship now and improve later.

chunks.heading: Ship an embarrassing V1 and don't fear a failed launch
chunks.text:
- He says the first version should make you cringe: "If you're not embarrassed by V1, you launched too late."
- Example: SuperX sat at $1k MRR for 10 months because the team kept "improving" before launching properly. The perfectionism cost time and momentum.
- His advice is to ship the embarrassing version and improve it publicly.
- On fear of failing: nobody will remember or care about a failed launch, and it won't become an industry topic. If it fails, nobody notices. If it succeeds, you win.

chunks.heading: Ideas, competition and execution
chunks.text:
- Tibo says your idea isn't unique. Someone else is building the same thing right now, which he sees as a good thing.
- The difference is who ships faster, markets better and iterates smarter. He says to stop protecting the idea and start executing it.
- "Someone's already doing this" is a validation signal, not a stop sign.
- Examples: scheduling tools already existed when he launched PostSyncer, and tweet schedulers existed when he built SuperX.
- His conclusion: competition proves market demand.

chunks.heading: Charge more
chunks.text:
- He says "Your prices are too low. I know this without seeing your product."
- Example: he raised Tweet Hunter prices 5x, revenue doubled and churn decreased. Higher prices attract better customers.
- His test: if nobody is complaining about price, you are leaving money on the table.

chunks.heading: Affiliate programs amplify growth, they don't create it
chunks.text:
- Tibo says an affiliate program won't save a failing product.
- Example: Outrank's affiliate program works because the product already had traction. The team amplified existing momentum and did not manufacture it from nothing.
- Order of operations: get growth first, then scale it with affiliates.

chunks.heading: Skip the paperwork and the courses, then act
chunks.text:
- He made his first $10k before registering any business entity. His advice is to set up an LLC when revenue actually matters, and not to use legal structure as an excuse to delay.
- On courses: every hour in a course is an hour not building, and "The market teaches faster than any curriculum."
- He adds that many course creators haven't built anything themselves, so courses often don't cover what you need to know.
- He says most advice, including his own newsletter, may not apply to you, so take principles rather than tactics.
- His closing point: "You don't have an information problem. You have an execution problem." The remedy is to build the thing, ship the product, talk to users and iterate fast.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo's playbook for buying SaaS products: open with a genuine compliment, ask easy questions, state buying intent, and follow up patiently. He then covers technical, financial, legal and marketing due diligence, plus tips like creative deal structuring and verifying Stripe data.

chunks.heading: How Tibo approaches the first conversation with a founder
chunks.text:
- He starts by reaching out to the maker of a product he likes and giving a genuine compliment. He wants the maker to feel unthreatened: "You are not trying to bring the product down or behaving like a shark."
- The aim of the opening is to build trust and a relationship, not to pitch.
- He then asks questions about the product's history, achievements and challenges. He notes that "Founders generally love to talk about what they created."
- His tip is to start with easy, low-effort questions and not to ask for full stats or analysis right away.
- Once the tone is set, he states clearly that he wants to buy. He believes transparency builds trust and sets expectations.

chunks.heading: Handling "No" and timing the approach
chunks.text:
- He treats an initial "No" as normal, because makers love what they built from scratch. He respects the decision and stays friendly to keep the door open.
- Timing matters. Founders of newly launched or very successful products often refuse to sell. When things start to go south, they become more willing to talk.
- He follows up periodically without being pushy. Owners remember interested buyers and often come back when they decide to sell.
- He watches industry news and the business's progress to spot challenges or turning points, and times his follow-ups around them.
- He does not rely on one seller. While discussing the acquisition of Typeframes, he was also talking to another video-editing SaaS, but no deal came of that one.
- His principle: "building relationships is the key. It's not just about the offer; it's about creating a long-term mutually beneficial partnership."

chunks.heading: Pricing and deal structure
chunks.text:
- He starts due diligence while terms are still being negotiated.
- He suggests looking at startups above your initial price limit. Buyers should also seek concessions through earn-outs, seller financing or loans.
- For small acquisitions, he starts due diligence with a simple letter of intent (LOI) sent over email.

chunks.heading: Technical due diligence
chunks.text:
- If you can't judge code quality yourself, he strongly recommends getting someone who can. Code quality and maintainability "will drastically change your acquisition experience."
- A premium SaaS should have clean, somewhat documented, annotated code. If it is a ticking time bomb, that should be part of the deal and lower the valuation. Bad code "could set you back a full year."
- Technical debt: understand its state and how hard the code will be to update. Ask for the ugliest and the most complex parts of the codebase.
- Infrastructure: ask about uptime over the last several months and the procedure for pushing code to production.
- Data security: understand how user data is protected and what authentication is in place.
- Integrations: they must fit business needs and future growth. Ask for all services, APIs and dependencies the product relies on.
- He quotes John Rush on uptime: most SaaS tools don't know their uptime stats, so ask them to set up monitoring and watch it for a month.

chunks.heading: Financial due diligence
chunks.text:
- Review the P&L and cross-check it against bank and credit card statements so income and expenses match.
- Getting view-only access to the seller's Stripe account is a deal-breaker for him if refused.
- Manually check the billing history of a few randomly chosen customers for anything odd.
- For consequential deal sizes, or without a finance background, hire an accountant or expert. A good broker like Acquire may have done preliminary due diligence.
- He suggests building your own P&L and comparing it with the founder's to find discrepancies: "it is worth the cost."
- A comprehensive report covers the P&L, balance sheet and cash flow, historical revenue and profit trends, and quality of earnings and net debt.
- Put churn "under a microscope": high churn means losing customers fast and paying for marketing.
- Check a sample of customers' demographics against what the seller claimed.
- Look at outliers such as spikes in new subscribers or churn, and ask why.

chunks.heading: Legal and marketing due diligence
chunks.text:
- Legal: get all running contracts, make sure the domain transfer is in the deal, and confirm the seller owns the property rights, trademarks and copyrights.
- Marketing: find out whether the seller pays to acquire customers and understand their CAC. Check where customers come from and whether that channel will stay active after the handover.
- Understand market size, the competitive landscape and trends such as shifts in demand, technology and regulation.
- Check whether growth is artificial because of heavy ad spend.
- He sees fewer explored acquisition channels as a plus, because that leaves more growth opportunities for the buyer.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo explains how he runs 5 products at $1M MRR: lock foundational decisions (price band, customer type, stack, positioning) once, and spend daily effort on execution. He also covers building systems instead of doing tasks, dogfooding, and the four things he optimizes every day.

chunks.heading: Pricing: one band, decided once, never revisited early
chunks.text:
- Tibo prices every product he builds in the same $40 to $100 per month range. He made this decision years ago and hasn't revisited it.
- That band attracts prosumers, "People with business intent." If the product helps their workflow they buy, with no negotiation or hand-holding.
- He argues this single decision drives the rest: subscription funnel design, account handling, team invitations, product complexity, support expectations and churn tolerance.
- Price bands map to customer types:
  - $10/month attracts consumers who "churn on vibes" and cancel because they "don't use it enough," even if it works perfectly.
  - $50/month attracts prosumers who need ROI. They stay if you deliver value and leave if you don't.
  - $500/month attracts businesses that expect personalized support, deep integration and implementation calls.
- Pick the band based on who you want to serve, then build everything around that customer type.
- Don't revisit pricing until $100k MRR or unless something big happens. Before that it's a distraction.
- Tibo says most founders spend 10 hours a month thinking about pricing and zero on whether they're solving the right problem for the right customer.
- His rule of thumb: spending more than 1 hour a month on pricing before $100k MRR means optimizing the wrong thing. Price it, ship it, see if people buy. Adjust only if nobody buys or everyone churns immediately.

chunks.heading: Decide foundations once, optimize execution daily
chunks.text:
- Tibo runs 5 products at a combined $1M MRR. His summary: "Foundations: once. Execution: daily."
- Foundations to pick once and keep consistent across products: customer type, pricing band, tech stack, funnel design, positioning.
- He says most decisions don't need to be unique per product, and optimization belongs at the execution layer (growth, product quality, systems), not the foundation layer.
- Founders stay stuck at under $5k/mo for years because they tweak foundations constantly (new pricing, new positioning, new stack) while growth stays flat, the product has bugs and support is manual. Tibo's framing: they start from zero every few weeks.
- Typical distractions he lists: tweaking pricing monthly, redesigning dashboards, chasing competitor features, switching tools.

chunks.heading: Build systems instead of doing tasks
chunks.text:
- Tibo says he doesn't do tasks anymore, he builds systems. The shift: stop asking "how do I do this task?" and ask "how do I make this task run without me?"
- His test for every task: "Will I need to do this again?" If yes, build a system (agent, hire or automation, "doesn't matter"). If no, do it manually once and move on.
- Examples he gives:
  - Instead of launching one campaign, build a campaign workflow and skill you can deploy on Claude any day.
  - Instead of manually onboarding one user, build an email-based onboarding flow that works for every user.
  - Instead of answering the same support question 50 times, write a mega doc and put an AI chatbot on the site.
- Repeatable tasks to systematize now:
  - Weekly metrics review becomes an automated dashboard.
  - Customer onboarding becomes an email sequence plus setup videos.
  - Feature requests become a public roadmap with voting.
  - Social posting becomes scheduled posts with templates.
  - Support becomes help docs plus an AI chatbot.
- Build these before you think you need to, because by the time you "need" to, "you're already drowning."
- This is how he runs 5 products: "I'm not doing 5x the work. I'm building 5x the systems." He says it matters even more for single-product founders, since "You can't scale if everything requires you."

chunks.heading: Use your own product (dogfooding)
chunks.text:
- Tibo uses every product he builds, multiple times a day when possible and at least once a week.
- He uses Revid.ai to create videos, Outrank.so for SEO content and PostSyncer.com to schedule posts. Each time he finds something to improve, and that becomes the roadmap.
- Benefits: spot problems before users complain, see opportunities competitors miss, and build what people need rather than what sounds good on the landing page.
- If you don't use your own product, either you're not your ICP (fix positioning) or the product isn't good enough yet (fix the product).
- The test question: "Would I pay for this if it wasn't mine?" If no, you have a problem.
- He calls dogfooding "not optional" and the difference between building features and building solutions.

chunks.heading: What Tibo optimizes every day
chunks.text:
- **Bottlenecks:** ask what's preventing growth right now, which is "the only thing that matters." Identify it, fix it, ignore the rest. Example: Outrank.so's bottleneck last month was content quality, since users said it sounded too robotic. The team fixed it and shipped an update this month that he says makes the SEO content at least 10x better.
- **User behavior:** compare what people do against what he expected, and ask why there's a gap. He watches PostHog session replays daily to see where users get stuck and where they succeed, and values what they actually do over what they say they do.
- **Systems breaking:** if something that used to run autonomously now needs manual intervention, treat it as a red flag, patch it immediately and don't let it grow.
- **New use cases:** watch how people use the product in ways he didn't anticipate, and see whether it can be generalized into a feature everyone can use.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Tibo explains why he sold two platform-dependent SaaS products, how revenue tripled after the sale by shipping more and running yearly challenges, and why lean teams, DM-based support and shipping messy content work. He also covers buying Typeframe with a revenue-share deal and managing AI and platform risk.

chunks.heading: Why Tibo builds: the early stage of a new product
chunks.text:
- He compares building to "playing Lego" at five years old. Money is not the driver; the best feeling is when people use something he built.
- He craves the earliest stage of a product, a mix of excitement and fear of not finding product-market fit. Once you have lived it, he says, "you desperately want to live it again."
- He uses that pressure as fuel. It pushes him to ship daily, change how people use the product, and look for new growth vectors.
- He recommends the book *It Doesn't Have to Be Crazy at Work* as a counterpoint to that culture, while running his own projects the opposite way.

chunks.heading: Why he and his co-founder sold Tweet Hunter and Taplio
chunks.text:
- The two products sold for over $10M, to Lempire (the company behind Lemlist).
- His co-founder wanted to sell more than he did. Tibo thought they could go much further.
- Platform dependence drove the decision. Tweet Hunter relied on Twitter, and Taplio relies on LinkedIn, plus a Chrome extension that pulls data beyond the public API.
- The SaaS was skyrocketing, but "we were definitely not getting a big money from the SaaS." Everything could collapse and they would get almost nothing from the success.
- He says the sale looked right once Twitter cut off API access, because it happened after the sale.

chunks.heading: Platform risk: the Twitter API cutoff and Chrome-extension products
chunks.text:
- In March 2023 Twitter announced developers would need to pay $42,000 per month for API access. It gave 30 days to transition and a form to fill in. Four days later their API access was cut with no warning.
- A few competitors were hit too. Tibo's team worked with them to find the right person at Twitter. One competitor tried to profit by trashing them publicly and grabbing their subscribers, which did not really work.
- After roughly 48 hours they reached the right contact, signed contracts fast, and got access back.
- Churn was under 1%. "It was more than an awful feeling than the actual truth."
- During the outage there was nothing to do except watch churn metrics. Because he builds in public, he "becomes the SaaS" and takes platform bugs personally.
- On Chrome extensions: he calls them a goldmine for indie makers. Big companies cannot allow teams to do "shady" things with private APIs, so solo founders face little competition there.
- His ethical line: does the product put the user's account at risk? For Taplio the answer is no, so he continues.

chunks.heading: Selling: why a French buyer, and how the deal closed
chunks.text:
